CHAPTER - I - INTRODUCTION 
1.1 Standing Committee on Rural Development and Panchayati Raj is one of the 
sixteen Departmentally Related Standing Committees of the Lok Sabha primarily 
entrusted with the mandatory task of examination of Demands for Grants for each 
financial year sought by the Ministry/Department under its purview while also 
scrutinizing the schemes under the administrative control of the concerned 
Ministry/Department. The present Report is on the examination of  the Demands for 
Grants of the Department of Rural Development ( Ministry of Rural Development) for 
the ensuing financial year 2023 -24 under Rule 331E(1)(a) of Rules of Procedure and 
Conduct of Business in Lok Sabha. 
1.2  Brief of the Ministry of Rural Development               
 The Department of Rural Development which  came into existence in October, 
1974 as a part of the Ministry of Food and  Agriculture was converted into a new 
Ministry of Rural Reconstruction on 18th August, 1979. The Ministry was renamed as 
the Ministry of Rural Development on 23rd January 1982. The Ministry of Rural 
Development was again converted into a Department in January 1985, under the 
Ministry of Agriculture & Rural Development. The Department was again upgraded as 
the Ministry of Rural Development on July 5, 1991. Another Department viz. 
Department of Wasteland Development was created under this Ministry on 2nd July 
1992. The Ministry was renamed in March 1995 as the Ministry of Rural Areas and 
Employment with three departments namely Department of Rural Employment and 
Poverty Alleviation, Rural Development and Wasteland Development.  
 
1.3 The Ministry was again renamed as the Ministry of Rural Development in 1999 
with three Departments i.e. Department of Rural Development, Department of Land 
Resources and Department of Drinking Water and Sanit ation. The Department of 
Drinking Water and Sanitation was separated from this Ministry on 13th July, 2011.  
 

2 
 
1.4 At present, the Ministry of Rural Development consists of two Departments, 
namely, (I) Department of Rural Development, and (II) Department of Land Resources. 
  
Objectives of Department of Rural Development    
The main objectives of the Ministry are classified as:  
i. Uplifting the deprived rural households through multidimensional 
support including for assets, livelihoods, infrastructure and services. 
Adopting a saturation approach and ensuring resilience to the families 
and communities.  
ii. Convergence of programmes and schemes. iii. Raising institutions of 
poor and forging partnerships with PRIs and other drivers of 
transformation. iv. Integrated and sustained monitoring of measurable 
outcomes.  
 
1.5 The vision and mission of the Ministry is sustainable and inclusive gro wth of 
rural India through a multipronged strategy for eradication of poverty by increasing 
livelihoods opportunities, providing social safety net and developing infrastructure for 
growth. This is expected to improve quality of life in rural India and to c orrect the 
developmental imbalances, aiming in the process, to reach out to most disadvantaged 
sections of the society. 
Major Programmes of Department of Rural Development  
 
(i) Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Scheme  
(MGNREGS) 
(ii) Pradhan Mantri Awaas Yojana - Gramin (PMAY-G) 
(iii) Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana (PMGSY) 
(iv) Deendayal Antyodaya Yojana - National Rural Livelihood Mission (DAY-
NRLM) 
(v) National Social Assistance Programme (NSAP) 
(vi) Saansad Aadarsh Gram Yojana (SAGY) 
 
1.6 The Detailed Demands for  Grants of the Ministry of Rural Development 
were laid in Lok Sabha on 7 th February, 2023. An allocation of Rs. 1,57,545 Crore 
has been made in the Budget Estimates of Demand No. 87 for the year 2023 -24. 
This allocation is 15.89% more than BE of 2022 -23 and 13.01% less than RE of

INTRODUCTION 
I, the Chairperson of the Standing Committee on Rural Development and 
Panchayati Raj (2024-2025) having been authorised by the Committee to submit the 
Report on their behalf, present the Tenth Report on ‘Functioning of National Institute of 
Rural Development and Panchayati Raj (NIRD&PR)’ of the Ministry of Rural 
Development (Department of Rural Development).  
2.  The Committee held briefing by the representatives of the Ministry of Rural 
Development (Department of Rural Development) on 17th March, 2025. 
3. The Report was considered and adopted by the Committee at their sitting held on 
16 June, 2025. 
4.  The Committee wish to express their thanks to the officials of the Ministry of 
Rural Development (Department of Rural Development) for placing before them the 
requisite material and their considered views in connection with the examination of the 
subject.  
5. The Committee would also like to place on record their deep sense of 
appreciation for the invaluable assistance rendered to them by the officials of Lok 
Sabha Secretariat attached to the Committee.

A. Introduction 
 
1.1 The 73rd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1992, marked a watershed moment in 
India's democratic decentralization by institutionalizing Panchayats as the third tier of 
governance. The Amendment empowered Panchayats to function as institutions of local 
self-government and entrusted them with the preparation and implementation of plans 
for economic development and social justice. Under this amendment, the Eleventh 
Schedule of the Constitution was introduced, listing 29 subjects under the jurisdiction of 
Panchayats. Several of these subjects are directly relevant to the "Clean and Green 
Village" theme, including: 
 
 Social forestry and farm forestry 
 Non-conventional energy sources 
 Sanitation 
 Minor irrigation, water management, and watershed development

INTRODUCTION 
I, the Chairperson of the Standing Committee on Rural Development & 
Panchayati Raj (2024-2025) having been authorised by the Committee to present 
the Report on their behalf, present the 4th Report on the action taken by the 
Government on the recommendations contained in the Thirty-Seventh Report of the 
Standing Committee on Rural Development and Panchayati Raj (17thLok Sabha) on 
‘Rural Employment through Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee 
Act (MGNREGA) – An insight into wage rates and other matters relating thereto’ 
(2023-24) of the Ministry of Rural Development (Department of Rural Development). 
2.  The Thirty-Seventh Report was presented to the Lok Sabha on 08.02.2024 
and was laid on the Table of Rajya Sabha on 08.02.2024. Replies of the 
Government to all the recommendations contained in the Report were received on 
12.06.2024. 
3.  The Report was considered and adopted by the Committee at their sitting held 
on 13.12.2024. 
4.  An analysis of the action taken by the Government on the recommendations 
contained in the Thirty-Seventh Report (17th Lok Sabha) of the Committee is given in 
Appendix-II.

INTRODUCTION 
I, the Chairperson of the Standing Committee on Rural Development & 
Panchayati Raj (2024-2025) having been authorised by the Committee to submit 
the Report on their behalf, present the Sixth Report on Demands for Grants 
(2025-26) of the Ministry of Rural Development (Department of Land Resources).  
2.  Demands for Grants have been examined by the Committee under Rule 
331E (1) (a) of the Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business in Lok Sabha. 
3.  The Committee took evidence of the representatives of the Department of 
Resources (Ministry of Rural Development) on 19th February, 2025. 
4. The Report was considered and adopted by the Committee at their sitting 
held on 10th March, 2025. 
5.  The Committee wish to express their thanks to the officials of the Ministry 
of Rural Development (Department of Land Resources) for placing before them 
the requisite material and their considered views in connection with the 
examination of the subject.  
6. The Committee would also like to place on record their deep sense of 
appreciation for the invaluable assistance rendered to them by the officials of Lok 
Sabha Secretariat attached to the Committee.

(BARC) and Nuclear Power Corporation of India Limited (NPCIL)”.

Energy (DAE). It serves approximately 150,000 new cancer patients annually, making it one of 
India‟s largest and most advanced cancer care institutions. The Committee visited TMC on 21 st 
September, 2025 as part of its study tour to Chandigarh and Mumbai from 19th to 2 2nd September 
2025 to explore the remarkable contributions being made by the institute in the field of cancer 
research and treatment, and to discuss the challenges and opportunities that lie ahead in advancing 
India‟s capabilities in these critical areas. 
3.  Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (BARC) is an R&D institution under the Department of 
Atomic Energy. Nuclear Power Corporation of India Limited (NPCIL) is a Public Sector Enterprise 
under the administrative control of the  Department of Atomic Energy (DAE) , responsible for 
design, construction, commissioning and operation of nuclear power reactors. The Committee 
visited BARC on 21 st September 2025 as part of its study tour to Chandigarh and Mumbai from

 behalf, present this Eleventh Report of the Committee. This Report deals with the Detailed Demands for Grants (1994-95) of the Department of Ocean Development.

 and the submissions made before it by the Secretary and other officials of the Department in the course of their oral evidence.
3. The Committee considered and adopted this report at its sitting held on the 15th April, 1994.

 Demands for Grants.

REPORT
            The Department of Ocean Development has proposed an outlay of Rs. 59 crores, which includes a Plan component of Rs. 46 crores and Non-plan component of
 Rs. 13 crores for the year 1994-95. This represents an increase of just Rs. 2.59 crores over that of the year 1993-94. In relative terms, there has been an increase of Rs. 3
 crores in plan outlay, which gets reflected in higher allocations being made for Marine Satellite Information Service, National Ocean Information System and National
 Institute of Ocean Technology vis-a-vis those made for these programmes during the year 1993-94; whereas in the Non-plan outlay, the expenditure is projected Rs. 41
 lakhs less. The comparative figures in terms of allocations for various programmes of the Department of Ocean Development for the years 1992-93, 1993-94 and 1994-
95 are given in    Annexure-I.
 
2.    The Committee before examining the outlay of the Department for the year 1994-95, vide Demand No. 87, went into the projected demand figures of the

 Department

INTRODUCTION
 
I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Science & Technology, Environment
 and Forests, having been authorized by the Committee, present its 154
th Report relating to Wild Life (Protection)
 Amendment *Bill 2005.  The Bill seeks to amend the Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972.
2.         In pursuance of the rules relating to the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committees, Hon’ble
 Chairman, Rajya Sabha **referred the Bill, as introduced in the Rajya Sabha on the 23rd December, 2005 and pending
 therein, to the Committee on the 29th December, 2005 for examination and report within 3 months.
3.         At it first meeting held on the 10th February, 2006, the Committee held internal discussion on the Bill.  At its
 second meeting held on the 21st February 2006, the Committee heard the presentation of the Secretary, Ministry of
 Environment and Forest on the Bill.  In its meetings held on 22nd and 23rd February 2006, it heard the views of the
 Experts on the Bill.  The Committee took clause-by-clause consideration of the Bill on the 1st and 7th March, 2006.
4.         The Committee heard the oral evidence of 3 experts to have better appreciation of the subject.  It also received
 one written submission from one of the experts (Annexure ‘A’).
5.         While considering the Bill, the Committee took note of the following documents/information placed before it:-
(i)         Background note on the Bill received from the Ministry of Environment &      Forests.
(ii)        The Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972.
Report of the Tiger Task Force.
Oral evidence and written submission tendered before the Committee.
Views of the Ministry of Environment & Forests and Ministry of Law & Justice.
6.         The Committee considered and adopted the Report in its meeting held on the 17
th March, 2006.
 7.        For the facility of reference and convenience, the observations and recommendations of the Committee have been
 given in bold letters in the body of the Report.
8.         The Committee expresses its gratitude to the Experts for their valuable suggestions on the Bill. The Committee is
 also thankful to the officials of the Ministry of Environment and Forest and Ministry of Law and Justice for assisting in
 its deliberations.
 
New Delhi P.G. NARAYANAN

            The Ministry of Environment and Fo rests is the nodal agency in the administrative structure o f 
the Central Government for the planning, promotion and coordinati on of environment and forestry
programmes. Within the overall framework of its ma ndate, the main activities of the Ministry include
conservation and survey of flora,  fauna, forests and wildlife, pr evention and control of pollution,
afforestation and regeneration of degraded areas, protection of the environment and ensuring the welfare
of animals. These tasks are sought to be fulf illed through environment impact assessment, eco-
regeneration, assistance to organizations implem enting environmental a nd forestry programmes,
enactment of environmental legi slation, formulation of envir onmental policies, promotion o f
environmental and forestry rese arch, extension, education and tr aining to augment the requisite
manpower, and dissemination of e nvironmental awareness among all sections of the country’s 
population.

and became a full fledged Department under Ministry of Science & Technology in 1986. 
The vision of the Department inter-alia includes creation of biotechnology tools and 
technologies that address the problems of agriculture productivity, food production, 
nutrition security, health care and environmenta l sustainability affecting the large section 
of the society, providing  new and emerging pr oducts and services at affordable prices, 
generating employment opportunities and ma king India globally competitive in the 
emerging bio-economy. The Department seeks to achieve its vision by facilitating 
emergence of a system that promotes ex cellence and sustains innovation through 
implementation of novel schemes/programmes and institutional mechanisms.

INTRODUCTION
I, the Chairman of the Committee on Science and Technology, Environment and Forests, having been authorised by the Committee to
 submit the Report on its behalf, present this Twenty Second Report, on the Demands for Grants pertaining to the Ministry of Environment
 and Forests for the year 1995-96 (Demand No. 22).
2. In its meetings held on April 6 and 20, 1995 the Committee considered the Demands for Grants of the Ministry of Environment and
 Forests on the basis of the documents made available to it and the submissions made before it by the Secretary and the other representatives
 of the Ministry.

Chairman, Committee on Science and Technology,
Environment and Forests
 
REPORT
The Ministry of Environment and Forests is the nodal agency at the national level for planning, promotion and co-ordination of
 environmental and forestry programmes . Its mandate includes survey and conservation of flora, fauna, forests and wildlife; prevention and
 control of pollution; afforestation and regeneration of degraded areas; and in general protection of the environment. Pursuant to this mandate,
 the tasks undertaken by the Ministry are: environmental impact assessment; eco-regeneration; assistance to organisations implementing
 environmental and forestry programs; enactment of environmental legislation; formulation of environmental policies; promotion of
 environmental and forestry . research, extension, education and training to augment the requisite manpower; dissemination of environmental
 information, creation of environmental awareness among all sections of the country's population; and international cooperation.
2. A total outlay of Rs. 435.41 crores for the year 1995-96 has been proposed, vide demand no. 22 for the Ministry of Environment and
 Forests to enable it to fulfill its mandate. The Plan component of this outlay is Rs. 370.50 crores and the Non-Plan component Rs. 64.91
 crores. The allocations for the year 1995-96 represent an increase of Rs. 10.50 crores in the Plan Sector and about Rs. 5 crores in the Non-
Plan Sector over the revised estimates for the year 1994-95. In terms of activity-wise allocations, the Plan allocations for forestry and wildlife
 have gone up from Rs. 203.09 crores to Rs 210.15 cr

and Technology, Environment and Forests, having been authorized by the Committee to present the
Report on its behalf, present this Two Hundred Thirtieth Report on Steps Taken by various sectors
of the Indian Economy to Control Pollution.
2. The Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Science and Technology,
Environment and Forests, decided to take up for consideration the subject ‘Steps Taken by various
sectors of the Indian Economy to Control Pollution’ and report thereon.
3. In this regard the Committee heard the views of the Secretaries, Ministries/Departments of
Environment and Forests, Coal, Mines, Steel, Power, Petroleum and Natural Gas, Heavy Industry,
Shipping (including Ports), Railways, Civil Aviation, Road Transport and Highways, Defence,
Defence Production, Health and Family Welfare, Agriculture, Urban Development, Chemicals and
Fertilizers (D/o Pharmaceuticals) and Tourism. The Committee, in all held 14 meetings and devoted
33.51 hours in the process of the consideration of the subject. The Committee also visited Mumbai,
Goa, Bengaluru, Visakhapatnam to get first hand information on the State of Pollution and measures
taken to mitigate it.
4. The Committee expresses its thanks to the officers of the Ministry of Environment and

 technologies through R&D programmes, promoting applications of electronics particularly export oriented, creation of
 infrastructure for standardisation , testing and quality certification, development of manpower resources and co-
ordination of various applications of electronics.

INTRODUCTION
I, the Chairperson of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Science &
Technology, Environment & Forests, having been authorized by the Committee to present the Report on its
behalf, present this Two Hundred Ninety-third Report on “Forest Fires and its Effect on Environment,
Forests, Bio-diversity and Wildlife and remedial/preventive measures”.
2. In its meeting held on the 31st May, 2016 the Committee heard the views of the Ministry of
Environment, Forest & Climate Change and National Disaster Response Force (NDRF) on the subject. The
Committee also undertook a study visit to Mussoorie, Katra and Shimla from 6th to 11th June, 2016 and
discussed the subject with the representatives of Union Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change,
NDRF and State Governments of Uttarakhand, Jammu & Kashmir and Himachal Pradesh and some NGOs/
members of civil society at these places.
3. The Committee expresses its thanks to the officers of the Ministry of Environment, Forest & Climate
Change; NDRF, State Governments of Uttarakhand, Jammu & Kashmir and Himachal Pradesh and members
of Civil Society/NGOs for placing before the Committee the required material and replying to the clarifications
sought by the Members on the subject.
4. In its meeting held on 15th December, 2016 the Committee considered the draft report and adopted
the same.

I, the Chairman of the Committee on Science & Technology, Environment & Forests, 
having been authorised by the Committee to submit the Report on its behalf, present this 
32nd Report on the Demands for Grants pertaining to the Department of Electronics for the 
year 1996-97. 
2. The Committee held in all one meeting on August 13, 1996. In the meeting held on 
13th August, 1996 while deliberating on the Demands for Grants of the Department of 
Electronics, the Committee sought detailed clarifications and explanations from the 
representatives of the Department of Electronics. The Committee wishes to express its 
thanks to the officers of the Department of Electronics and the Planning Commission for 
placing before it the requisite material and answering the queries raised by Members on 
various aspects of the Electronics programme and related aspects to enable it to scrutinise 
the Demands for Grants . 
3. The Committee considered and adopted its draft report at its meeting held on 23rd 
August, 1996. 
4. Electronics, in one form or the other, is the backbone of the entire industrial activity. 
Department of Electronics (DOE) is the promotional department of Government of India 
committed to development of Indian industry and applications of IT and electronics in the 
general walk of life in India. DOE is committed to development of technology tools and 
applications and in geheral to the proper utilisation of technology in society in public. DOE 
does technology forecasting exercise in which technology plays profound impact on society 
and people. Computer networking was one such area identified 10 years ago by DOE before 
it was perceived by other agencies in the country. In a similar approach DOE initiated a 
programme calle.d ERNET to fo~s on development of national capability in computer 
network in the country. It has led to the movement similar to Internet which was infact not 
known in those days. DOE has played a pioneer role in publidsing E-Mail and subsequently 
providing it in the country. 
5. While DOE is the promotional agency for electronics in the country, Department of 
Telecommunications (DOT) is the nodal agency in the field of telecommunications and it has 
played a big role in the development of telecommunications in the country. As such DOT 
and DOE are complimentary agencies in furthering the total area on IT, electronics and 
telecommunications. Therefore, the two agencies have to work together to converge at the 
technology level in telecommunications and IT electronics. 
6. DOE has ~hree public sector undertakings namely CMC, ET &T and SCL. Besides, a 
large number of societies including C-DAC, ER&DC, STPI, SAMEER, CEDT , DOEACC, 
NCST. DOE also has a large outfit of STQC laboratories all over the country. These 
agencies act as the anns of the Department in fulfilling its goals.

I, the Chairman of the Committee on Science & Technology, Environment & Forests, 
having been authorised by the Committee to submit the Report on its behalf , present this 
33rd Report on the Demands for Grants pertaining to the Department of Space ft. r the year 
1996-97 (Demand No. 91). 
2. The Committee held in aJI one meeting on August 9, 1996. In the meeting held on 
August 9, 1996, while deliberating on the Demands for Grants of the Department of Space, 
the Committee sought detailed clarifications and explanations from the representatives of the 
Departm ent of Space. The Committee wishes to express its thanks to the officers of the 
Department of Space for placing before it the requisite material and answering the queries 
raised by Members on various aspects of the Space Programme and related aspects to enable 
it to scrutinise the Demands for Grants. 
3. The Committee considered and adopted a draft report at its meeting held on August 
23, 1996. 
4. The Indian Space Programme assumes significance in the context of advances made 
in the space technology and its varied applications in the field of national development on a 
sustainable basis in key areas like communication, meteorology, natural resources 
management and environmental monitoring, in a timely, cost effective and self-reliant 
manner. Remarkable developments in space technology and its application have thus 
contributed significantly towards utilization of our natural resources. 
5. The setting up of the Thumba Equatorial Rocket Launching Station (TERLS) in 
early sixties marked the beginning of the Indian Space Programme. The Space Commission 
and the Department of Space were established by the Government in 1972 with a view to 
promote unified development and application of space science and technology for identified 
national objectives. Many advanced countries, which pursued Space programme~ since 1950s, 
were motivated by the desire to be at the forefront of exploration and Science to stay at the 
cutting edge of technology in aerospace, to establish human presence in space and to exploit 
commercially the benefits that accrued from these efforts . It is because space provides 
advantage point to view the planet Earth in its totality and to facilitate connectivity, cutting 
across physical barriers and trans nat_ional boundaries. 
6. The thrust of our Space Programme is towards the goal of self-reliant use of space 
technology for national development mainly in the following areas: 
(a) Satellite communications for various applications,

monitoring and meteorological services, and

1, the Chairman of the Committee on Science and Technology, Environment and 
Forests, having been authorised by the Committee to submit the report on its behalf, present 
this 34th Report of the Committee. This Report deals with the Demands for Grants 
pertaining to Department of Biotechnology (Ministry of Science & Technology) for the year 
1996-97 (Demand No. 76). 
2. In the meeting of the Committee held on the 13th August, 1996, the representatives 
of the Department of Biotechnology gave an overview of the various activities of the 
Department and the Committee sought clarifications on the various aspects of the 
functioning of the Department of Biotechnology. 
3. The Committee wishes to express its thanks to the officers of the Department of 
Biotechnology for their cooperation and answering the queries raised by Hon'ble Members 
on various aspects on programmes initiated by the Department. 
4~ The Committee considered and adopted the draft report at its meeting held on the 
23rd August, 1996. 
5. The world has witnessed spectacular advances in the field of biotechnology in the last 
43 years after the Nobel Prize discovery of the structure and D~A by Watson and Crick, in 
1993. The field was regarded as the greatest individual enterprise of the humankind in this 
century. It has revolutionised the industrial scenario, specially, the pharmaceutical industry 
all over the world, in particular, in advanced countries. Biotechnology is a science which 
uses the living organisms to make or modify a product-to improve plants or animals and 
microorganisms for specific uses. It aims at harnessing the genetic diversity in the living 
organisms for manufacture of useful products and production of strains of microbes, plants 
and animals with improved qualities. 
6. The need to accelerate the pace of research in biotechnology was felt in India.

4. The Department of Ocean Development was established ia 1981 as a part of Cabinet

REPORT 
I, the Chairman of the Committee on Science and Technology, Environment & Forests 
having been authorised by the Committee to present the report on its behalf, present the 
Thirty-sixth Report, on the Demands for Grants pertaining to the Department of Scientific 
and Industrial Research for the year 1996-97 (Demand No. 75). 
2. In its meetings held on 13th and 22nd August, 1996 the Committee discussed in detail 
the Demands for Grants of the Department of Scientific and Industrial Research on the 
basis of documents made av·ailable to it and the submissions made before it by the Secretary 
of the Department and the other representatives of the Department. 
3. The Committee expresses its thanks to the officers of the Department for replying to 
the clarifications sought by the Hon'ble Members and placing before it the required material 
to enable the Committee to scrutinise the Demands for Grants of the Department of 
Scientific and Industrial Research. 
4. The Committee considered and adopted the Report at its meeting held on 
September 3, 1996. 
5. The thrust of the programmes and activities of the Department of Scientific and 
Industrial Research (DSIR) is on the activities of Council of Scientific and Industrial 
Research (CSIR)- a premier Science and Technology (S&T) agency with a network of 40 
national laboratories, two complexes and 81 Extension and Regional Centres spread all over 
the country, Technology Promotion, Development, Utilisation and Transfer (TPDU) and 
National Information System for Science and Technology (NISSAT). 
6. Other major programmes of the Department include Research and Development by 
Industry (RDI) consisting of in-house R & D in Industry, Scientific and Industrial Research 
Organisations (SIROs) and Fiscal ·Incentives for Scientific Research; Programme Aimed at 
Technological Self Reliance {PATSER) consisting of development of new or improved 
technologies. Development of speciaVcustom built capital goods, absorption and adaptation 
of improved technology, studies and interactions concerning Technology Evaluation and pre­
feasibility reports of major sectors/products; Scheme to Enhance the Efficacy of Transfer of 
Technology (SEETOT) consisting of National Register of Foreign Collaborations (NRFC), 
Industrial Technology, Transfer and Trading in Technology (TA TT), Linkages with 
International Organisations including Asian and Pacific Centres for Transfer of Technology 
(APCIT) and Promotion and Support to Consultancy Services (PSCS) including the 
Consultancy Development Centre (CDC) and two Public Enterprises viz. National Research 
Development Corporation (NRDC) and Central Electronics Limited (CEL) engaged in the 
commercialisation of indigeneously developed technologies.

1, the Chairman of the Committee on Science and Technology, Environment and 
Forests, having been authorised by the Committee to present the report on its behalf. 
present the Thirty-seventh Report, on the Demands for Grants pertaining to the Ministry of 
Environment and Forests for the year 1996-97 (Demand No. 22). 
2. In its meeting held on 8th and 22nd August, 1996 the Committee discussed in detail 
the Demands for Grants of the Ministry of Environment and Forests on the basis of 
documents made available and the submissions made before it by the Secretary and other 
officials of the Department. 
3. The Committee thanks the officers of the Ministry for replying to the clarifications 
sought by the Hon'ble Members and placing before it the required material to enable the 
Committee to scrutinise the Demands for Grants of the Ministry of Environment and 
Forests . 
4. The Committee considered and adopted the Report at its meeting held on 9th 
September , 1996. 
5. India , the seventh largest country (area 329 million ha.) in the world, covers 2% of 
land area, while supporting 16% of human population (900 million) and 15% of cattle 
population (480 million): It is one of the 12 mega bio-diversity countries, commanding 7% 
of the world bio-diversity. India has merely 1% of forest area and 112% of grazing land of 
the world. Per capita forest area in the country works out to 0.08 ha. as against global 
average of about 1.00 ha. Forests in the country are thus subjected to enormous biotic 
pressures. 
6. The very existence of the country and its all-round progress is greatly dependent on 
sustainable development. lt is, therefore, vital 'that a check is exercised on the environment . 
Our hoary traditions of environmental conservation which have inculcated in us a deep 
reverence for nature and an awareness of the age-old truth that all forms of life, be it 
human, animal or plant are inter-woven and any damage to one may cause serious threat to 
the rest. The age-old traditions of environment protection and reverence to the mother 
nature have been given prominence in our national priorities. It is therefore duty of 
everyone of us to protect and improve the natural environment, including forest, lakes, 
rivers and wildlife and to have compassion for living creatures. However, it is being noticed 
that as a result of economic progress pressure is steadily increasing on the environment and 
the natural resources. 
7. Over the years , the countries have realised the importance of protecting environment 
and preserving forests for the welfare and good of the mankind . The organisation of the 
Stockholm Conference on Environment and Development in 1972 further provided impetus 
to this realisation amongst the countries, whether developed or developing. In India, the 
Departm ent of Environment, as a separate department, was set up towards the end of 1980.

scarcities and shortages led to inventions. The men behind these inventions were not always 
intellectuals hailing from affluent families. Instead, they came from ordinary walks of life and in 
many cases were illiterate and so poor that they did not have even two square meals a day. They 
burnt mid-night oil in order to help the mankind with the benefit of their inventions. They 
followed the ideals enshrined in what Sir Winston Churchill described in following woi:ds:-
"Heights of the great men were not attained in a single flight, they came up toiling upwards when 
their companions slept in the night" 
The domain of inventions is thus not the property of any intellectuals or enlightened or 
affluent sections of the Society alone. It belongs to one and all. 
Shri P. Ramar Pillai who shot in the news sometime back comes from ordinary walk of life. 
He was reported to have invented what he described as "Herbal Fuel". This gave him a world­

research and treatment, and to discuss the challenges and opportunities that lie ahead in advancing 
India‟s capabilities in these critical areas.

I, the Chairman of the Committee on Science and Technology, Environment and Forests, having been authorised by the
 Committee to submit the report on its behalf present this 42nd Report of the Committee. The report is based on the 'Mid-Term
 Appraisal' of the Programmes and Functioning of the Department of Space, undertaken by the Committee.
2. In the meeting of the Committee held on the 16th January, 1997, the Secretary and other officials of the Department of
 Space gave an overview of the activities of the Department and the Committee sought clarifications on the various !aspects on the
 performance and functioning of the Department during the year 1996-97 particularly in the fields of Research and Development,
 application of Satellite Technology for Rural Uplift and allied areas and its financial aspects.
3. The Committee wishes to express its thanks to the officers of the Department of Space for their co-operation and answering
 the queries raised by Members on various aspects of the programmes and initiatives taken by the Department.
4. The Committee considered and adopted the draft report at its meeting held on the 5th March, 1997.
5. The Secretary, Department of Space in his presentation before the Committee, gave a graphic account of the performances
 and achievements of the Department of Space during the year 1996-97 and an overview of the thrust areas in which the
 Department is presently engaged in pursuance of the national objectives of attaining the goal of total self-reliant use of space
 technology for National Development, which has not only revolutionised the present but promises to shape our future. Since the
 modest beginning in 1972 the Department of Space and the autonomous institutions functioning under the Department have been
 making consistent efforts in formulation of policy statements on guidelines on Space programmes which are carried out through

this Fifty-first Report of the Committee. This Report deals with the Demands for Grants 
pertaining to Department of Biotechnology (Ministry of Science & Technology) for the year 
1997-98 (Demand No. 76). 
2. In the meeting of the Committee held on the 15th April, 1997, the representatives of 
the Department of Biotechnology gave an overview of the. various activities of the 
Department and the Committee sought clarification on the various aspects of the functioning 
of the Department of Biotechnology. 
3. The Committee considered and adopted the draft report at its meeting held on 8th 
May, 1997. 
4. The world has witnessed spectacular advances in the fields of biotechnology during 
the last 44 years after the discovery of the structure and DNA by Watson and Crick, in 
1953, for which they were awarded Nobel Prize in Medicines and Physiology. The field was 
regarded as the greatest individual enterprise of the humankind. It has revolutionised the 
industrial scenario, especially, the pharmaceutical industry all over the world, particularly in 
technologically advanced countries. Biotechnology is a science which uses the living 
organisms to make or modify a product-to improve plants or animals and microorganisms for 
specific uses. It aims at harnessing the genetic diversity in the living organisms for 
manufacture of useful products and production of strains of microbes, plants and animals 
with improved qualities. 
5. The Department of Biotechnology, estabished in 1986, is expected to give a greater 
impetus to the development of biotechnology in the country. The objectives of the 
Department include development of products and processes and technologies whose large­
scale applications would result in societal and economic benefits.

67th Report on Demands for Grants of Department of Electronics
 
The Department of Electronics (DOE)  is responsible for the development of the electronics industry formulation,
 promoting application  of electronics and informative technology,  implementation and review of various programmes/schemes
 in the field of electronics.  These schemes are implemented both in-house as well as through PSUs /Societies  under DOE and
 also through various sponsored programmes being funded under R&D.
2.         The Department is a medium not only to provide a focal point of Government’s attention to electronics sector and also to
 function as a coordinator within and outside the Government, but is also responsible for bringing the benefits of electronics to
 every walk of life, and play a catalytic role to make the Indian Electronics Industry a global player  in the light of the new
 Industrial and Trade Policy.
3.         With delicensing of the entire electronics industry (except aerospace and defence electronics), liberalisation in foreign
 investment and Export-Import policies, the country is witnessing new investments, restructuring of existing activities,
 diversification of the product range and an intensely  competitive environment.  All the renowned global brands have either
 established production facilities in the country or are present in the market through technical/financial collaborations, thus
 giving consumer a wider choice in terms of product features, technology quality and competitive prices.
4.         The thrust , according to  DOE, during the Ninth Plan, would be on Export, Employment and productivity-led growth of
 Electronics and Information Technology.  The electronics and Information Technology sector has the propensity to increase the
 overall growth rate to higher level.
5.            Electronics is the fast growing sector of the Indian industry.  During the Eighth Plan, the electronics industry had a
 cumulative annual growth of 20 per cent in production and over 40 per cent in exports.  The electronics industry achieved a
 production level of Rs. 32,070 crores and an export performance of Rs. 9, 500 crores during the year 1997-98 and is likely to
 achieve a production level of Rs. 41,000 crores during the year 1998-99 registering a growth of over 28% and export
 performance of Rs.12800/- showing a net increase of 70 per cent.  A goal of annual electronics production of Rs. 1,38,350
 crores and exports of about Rs. 49,000 crores has been set for the terminal year of the Ninth Plan (2001-02), representing a
 growth rate of 39% and 52% respectively.

 was to the tune of Rs.  679.38 crores .  An allocation of Rs. 897.37 crores has been made available for the 9 th Five Year Plan

 769.57 crores  have been spent and left over allocation  is only Rs. 127.8 crores and the share of Budgetary support spent so far

Sixty-Eighth   Report on Demands for Grants (1999-2000)
of the Department of Space
 
            India’s Space Programme, since its inception in the early sixties, has been guided by a vision which laid emphasis on the
 application of space technology for finding solution to the problems of man and society thereby establishing a viable & self
 reliant space programme.  From the very beginning, long-range plans have been drawn up to steer the programme effectively
 ensuring appropriate linkages among the application needs, satellite missions, launch vehicle capabilities and technology
 development.  Over the last three-and-half decades, significant progress has been made  in  space technology for building
 world-class satellites for communications and remote sensing; for launching the remote sensing satellites from India with
 indigenous launch vehicle; and providing the benefits of space technology to improve the quality of life at the grass root level,
 thus contributing to several areas of national development.
2.         In tune with the goal of self reliant use of space technology for national development, the thrust areas of the Indian
 Space Programme include:-
(a)        satellite  based communication for various applications.
(b)        satellite based remote sensing for resources survey, management and environmental monitoring;
(c)        meteorological applications; and
(d)        development and operationalisation of indigenous and launch vehicles for providing these space services.
3.         The Department of Space (DOS) is responsible for implementing the policies framed by the Space Commission.  The
 policies are carried out through the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) and the three Grant in aid institutions, viz. the
 National Remote Sensing Agency (NRSA), the Physical Research Laboratory (PRL) and the National Mesosphere-
Stratosphere-Troposphere Radar Facility (NMRF).
4.         The cumulative expenditure on space research till the end of Eighth Plan period i.e. from the inception in 1962-63 to
 1996-97, is Rs.7431.67 crore.  During the Eighth Plan, most of the programmatic targets and missions planned have been
 achieved. The total expenditure incurred is Rs.3928.53 crore (Plan Rs.3155.74 crore and Non-Plan Rs.772.79 crore). The major
 missions achieved are INSAT-2B, INSAT-2C, INSAT-2D, IRS-1E, IRS-P2, IRS-1C, IRS-P3, SROSS-C1 and SROSS-C2.
 Besides, considerable progress in the areas like development of indigenous cryogenic engine and stage for the GSLV
 programme, technological development for indigenisation of strategic and critical sub-systems & components and setting up of
 facilities for realisation of inertial systems and electro-optical systems have been achieved. 
5.         The Committee was informed that the Planning Commission has allocated a Plan outlay of Rs.6511.72 crore, against
 their earlier communication of Rs.7100.00 crore and the Non-Plan outlay of Rs.1200 crore for the Ninth Plan period. Thus, the
 total outlay for the Ninth Plan is Rs.7711.72 crore. However, the actual Plan budgetary allocation would be decided annually
 based on the programmatic requirements.
6.         The programme directions and the programmatic targets for the Ninth Plan have been formulated after extensive
 interactions and consultations with user Ministries. The major missions planned for the Ninth Plan to realise the programmatic
 targets have been indicated in Annexure-I. While the basic vision would continue to be the large scale application of space
 technology for finding solutions to the problems of man and society, the programme would respond effectively to the dynamic
 and complex problems of the coming years. The   major programmes planned include (i) operationalisation of Geosynchronous
 Satellite Launch Vehicle (GSLV) towards achievement of self-reliance in launching communication satellites;  (ii) providing
 additional and newer operational communication satellite services to meet the increasing national needs;  (iii) building earth
 observation systems for wide range of applications related to land, water and ocean resources as well as atmospheric
 observations; (iv) establishing the GRAMSAT programme for integrating the potentials of satellite communication and remote
 sensing for rural development including the tele-education and tele-health; (v) establishing new communication services for
 Digital Audio and Data Broadcasting and Direct to Home TV services; (vi) establishing a viable system for Disaster
 Management through Earth observation, satellite-based communications, conventional survey information and local networks;
 (vii) research and development as well as technology development; and (viii) enhanced interface between Indian industry and

69th Report on Demands for Grants (1999-2000)of the Department
of Scientific and Industrial Research
 
The Department of Scientific and Industrial Research which forms a part of the Ministry of Science and Technology
 comprises of activities of Departmental Schemes viz. Research and Development by Industry (RDI), Programme
 Aimed at Technological Self Reliance (PASTER), Scheme to Enhance the Efficacy of Transfer of Technology
 (SEETOT), National Information System for Science and Technology (NISSAT) and management of the public sector
 undertaking, National Research Development Corporation (NRDC) and Central Electronics Limited (CEL). The long
 term objective of the programme on Research by Industry and Technology Transfer is technological self-reliance and
 the short term objectives are promotion of R&D by Industry and enhancing efficacy of technology transfer, both
 domestic and foreign. Issues addressed in these programmes include identification of technological gaps, making
 investment in R&D by Industry attractive and productive, development and commercialisation of domestic
 technologies through. In – house R&D in industry and R&D by public funded laboratories coupled with industry. The
 Department also looks after matters concerning the Council of Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR) which
 functions as a registered society and has a network of 40 laboratories and 81 field stations/extension centres/regional
 centres located all over the country that undertake R&D in various science and technology areas and disciplines.
2. The Secretary explained the achievements of the National Laboratories under the CSIR, in the fields of Aerospace,
 Biology and Biotechnology, Chemicals, Drugs and Pharmaceuticals, Earth resources and Natural hazards mitigation,
 Ecology and Environment, Food and Food Processing etc. which have tangible impact on the socio-economy sectors,
 during the Eighth Five Year Plan and informed about the new projects which the Department proposes to undertake
 during the year 1999-2000.
3. The Secretary also gave a brief presentation on the recent earthquake having an epicentre in the Chamoli region of
 Uttar Pradesh. The Committee enquired about the efforts made by the Department to arrest the damage and
 rehabilitation plans. The Committee specifically wanted to know whether any lead has been made for scientifically
 predicting earthquake. The Committee was informed that within CSIR a National Geophysical research Institute,
 Hyderabad and Central building Research Institute, Roorke are working for minimising the damage after an earthquake.
 As regards, predicting earthquakes, it was stated that as of today, there is no scientifically accepted method available to
 predict earthquakes accurately enough to be of help in saving human lives as there are no well established precursors
 which precede earthquake. A member pointed out that such an event in China was once preceded by strange behaviour
 of animals which led an elder to forecast that an earthquake was about to come and city was got vacated which helped
 minimise the damage. However, it is possible today to broadly work out the earthquake hazard in terms of accelerations
 that may occur at a given region based on the previous earthquake records. Then, on the basis of local geology and
 several other factors, it is possible to carry out mico zoning which indicates the kind of acceleration that would be
 expected in areas at a scale of a few hectares to a few square kilometres. Thereafter retrofitting of vulnerable structures
 can be done to save non engineered structures.
BUDGETARY ALLOCATIONS
4. The financial allocation for the Department of Scientific and Industrial Research for the year 1999-2000 is Rs.820.46
 crores as against Rs.737.46 crores in the R.E. of 1998-99 and Rs.638.00 crores in the B. E. of 1998-99 . Thus represents
 an increase in Rs.83.00 crores over the revised estimates and Rs.182.46 crores over the B.E. of 1998-99.(ANNEXURE
 )

REPORT
The Chairman, Rajya Sabha in pursuance of the rules relating to the Department-related Parliamentary Standing
 Committees, referred* the Semiconductor Integrated Circuits Layout-Design Bill, 1999, as introduced in the Rajya
 Sabha on the 20 th December, 1999, and pending therein, to the Committee for examination and Report by the 15 th
 February, 2000.
2. The above reference was considered by the Committee in its meetings held on 8 th February, 2000. After some
 discussion the Committee felt that it would not be possible for it to complete the examination of the provisions of the
 Semiconductor Integrated Circuits Layout Bill-1999 ** and submit its report within the stipulated time i.e.15th
 February, 2000. Accordingly, Chairman, Rajya Sabha was requested to grant extension of time to the Committee, upto
 the 29th day of February, 2000, for presentation of its report on the Bill. The request for extension of time was granted
 and notified in the Rajya Sabha Bulletin Part II dated the 23rd February,2000.
3. Electronics and Information Technology is one of the fastest growing sectors that has played a significant role in the
 world economy. This was primarily due to the advancement in the filed of electronics, computers and
 telecommunications. Microelectronics has rightly been recognized as a core strategic technology world over, especially
 for the Information Technology (IT) based society. Design of Integrated Circuit (IC) required considerable expertise
 and several hundreds of man-years of effort depending on the complexity. Such efforts culminate into the layouts for
 ICs, which are used for fabricating the ICs in the fabrication plants. In order to encourage continued investment in
 R&D leading to technological advancements in the field of microelectronics, protection of Intellectual Property Rights
 is of utmost importance.
4. The question regarding the type of the protection to be given to the layout design of Integrated Circuits is relatively
 new. Although prefabricated components of electrical circuitry have been used for a long time in the manufacture of
 electrical equipment (for example radios) large scale integration of a multitude of electrical functions in a very small
 component became possible only a few years ago as a result of advances in Semiconductor Technology. Integrated
 Circuits are manufactured in accordance with very detailed plans or "Layout designs".
transistors were fabricated and packaged separately and then connected on a board to realise on electrical circuit. With
 the advances in microelectronics technology, it has become possible to
______________________________________________________________________________
* Rajya Sabha Parliamentary Bulletin Part II, dated the 21st January, 2000.
** Annexure.
integrate several such devices on a small chip of semiconducting material. Such circuits are, therefore, called Integrated
 Circuits (ICs).
5. "Integrated Circuit" means a product in its final form or an intermediate form, in which the elements, at least one of
 which is an active element, and some or all of one of the connections are integrally formed in and which is intended to
 perform on electronic function.
"Layout Design" means the three – dimensional disposition, at least one
of which is an active element and of some or all of the interconnections of an integrated circuit, or such a three
 dimensional disposition prepared for an integrated circuit is intended for manufacture.
6. A layout-design of integrated circuit is a creation of human mind. It is the result of an enormous investment, both in
 terms of time of highly qualified experts and financial investment. There is a continuing need for the creation of new
 layout-designs which reduce the dimensions of existing integrated circuits and simultaneously increase their functions.

REPORT 71
file:///C/Users/user/Desktop/pri/Committee%20on%20S%20and%20T,%20Env.%20and%20Forests/71report.htm[29-08-2018 16:14:12]
 The smaller an integrated circuit, the less is the material needed for its manufacture, and smaller is the space needed to
 accommodate it. Integrated Circuits are utilized in a large range of products, including articles of mass consumption,
 such as watches, television sets, washing machines, automobiles, etc., as well as sophisticated data processing
 equipment.
Whereas the creation of a new layout-design for an integrated circuit involves an
important investment, the copying of such a layout design may cost only a fraction of that investment. Copying may be
 done by photographing each layer of an integrated circuit and preparing masks for the protection of the integrated
 circuit on the basis of the photographs obtained. The possibility of such copying is the main reason for the introduction
 of legislation for the protection of layout designs.

I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Science & Technology, Environment & Forests,
 having been authorised by the Committee to present the Report on its behalf, present this Seventy-third Report of the Committee.  This
 Report deals with  the detailed Demands for Grants (2000-2001) of the Department of Scientific and Industrial Research (Ministry of
 Science and Technology) (Demand No.74).
 
2.         In the meeting of the Committee held on the 31st March, 2000 the Secretary and other Officers of the Department of Scientific and
 Industrial Research gave an overview of the various activities of the Department and the Members sought clarifications on various
 aspects of the performance of the Department to enable it to scrutinise the Demands for Grants.
 
3.     The Committee expresses its thanks to the Officers of the Department for replying to the clarifications sought by the Members and
 placing before it the required material to enable the Committee to scrutinise the Demands for Grants of the Department of Scientific and
 Industrial Research.
 
4.         The Committee considered and adopted the Report at its meeting held on 18
th April, 2000.
 
 
New Delhi

R E P O R T
 
 The mandate of the Ministry of Environment and Forests entails planning, promotion and coordination of environment
 and forestry programmes. The main activities of the Ministry relate to conservation and control of pollution,
 afforestation and regeneration of forests in degraded areas, protection and conservation of forests, wildlife and
 protection of environment. The tasks are sought to be achieved through environmental impact assessment, eco-
regeneration, assistance to organisations implementing environmental and forestry programmes, enactment of
 environmental legislation, formulation of environmental policies, promotion of environmental and forestry research,
 extension, education and training to augment the requisite manpower, dissemination of environmental awareness
 among all sectors of the country’s population. The activities of the Ministry are divided in four major sectors, i.e.
1. Environment,
2. National River Conservation Directorate,
3. Forests and Wildlife and
4. National Afforestation and Eco-Development Board.
 
NINTH PLAN AND ANNUAL PLANS
2. The total central sector ninth plan (1997-2002) allocation is Rs.489361.58 crores. Out of this, the share of Ministry of
 Environment and Forests is only Rs.3013.84 crores, i.e. only 0.61% of the total central plan outlay. The actual
 expenditure of the Ministry in 1998-99 was Rs.498.05 crores against the revised estimate of rs.468.00 crores. An
 allocation of Rs.7000.00 crores was made for 1999-2000. It was revised by the Ministry of Finance to Rs.610 crores at
 R.E. stage, Ministry is expected to spend Rs.610.00 crores during 1999-2000 which is 22.48% higher then 1998-99.

79th Report on the Information Technology Bill, 1999
 
 The Chairman, Rajya Sabha in pursuance of the rules relating to the Department-related Parliamentary Standing
 Committees, referred* the Information Technology Bill, 1999**, as introduced in the Lok Sabha on 16 th December,
 1999 and pending therein, to the Standing Committee on Science & Technology, Environment & Forests for
 examination and Report.
2. In the present day world it has been the electronics and now the Information Technology (IT) which influence our life
 the most. There is hardly any area of human endeavour where electronic gadgets have not reached. There is barely any
 industry which does not depend, for its efficiency and productivity, on the application of electronics in its different
 manifestations. Technology has emerged as the vehicle of rapid change in the work culture and the way mankind
 communicates in the century. India has been no exception to this phenomenon. Whether in the field of
 telecommunications, roads, ports or air travel, the hallmark has been more efficient and cost effective technology. Thus
 from slow-moving majestic automobiles the country has moved to smart and fast technologies which have given us
 much more advanced vehicles, coal guzzling steam locomotives which have been replaced by electric traction engines.
3. Information Technology is a product of information age and technology. It is a vehicle for future development,
 opportunities, challenges and competition that enables faster collection and dissemination of information. In the history
 of civilization, no work of science has had so comprehensive an impact on human development as IT. Undoubtedly, IT
 has been the greatest changing agent of this century and promises to play its role even more dramatically in the times to
 come. IT is changing every aspect of human life, breaking old barriers and building new inter connections in the
 emerging global village and becoming the chief determinant of progress of nations and that of individuals. IT is being
 meaningfully employed in railways and airlines, banking, insurance, weather forecasting, radio astronomy, molecular
 biology, aerodynamics, etc. thereby reducing the fatigue and increasing the productivity and efficiency. And in
 education too, IT has a vital role. A large variety of software is available to cater to self-learning and evaluation on
 various subjects.
4. IT is a broad term covering the entire gamut of managing and processing information. Computer hardware, software
 and internet are the tools for the systems that have been designed, developed, supported or managed by IT
 professionals. The discovery of computers and subsequent development of the technology popularly known as
 information technology is one of the most significant achievements of the 20
th century. The role of IT as an instrument
 for progress and development has been acknowledged widely and is expected to bring in major social and economic
 benefits for the mankind and accelerate the process of development.
 
 
 
* Rajya Sabha Parliamentary Bulletin Part II, dated the 14
th January, 2000
** Annexure

5. Andhra Pradesh is an example of how the States in the country can incorporate IT in the day-to-day functioning of the
 Government and re-engineer the manner in which services are provided to citizens. Under its ‘One-stop non-stop’
 approach, a pilot project called Twin cities Integrated Network Service (TWINS) integrated 18 services of six
 departments over one counter. It provides fast and easy access to Government services, makes the access to
 Government much simpler and can also cut down on corruption. It would be naive, of course, to suggest IT as the
 ultimate panacea for corruption, which may find ingenious ways to beat new technology.
6. Today, among the major Asian industrialized countries, India has abundant technically skilled manpower towards
 global IT development. IT is the fastest emerging industrial segment in the country. During the last decade, IT sector
 has registered an unprecedented growth. All the renowned global brands have either established production facilities in
 the country or are present in the market through technical/financial collaborations, thus giving consumer a wider choice
 of products in terms of features, quality and prices.

Introduction
 
I, the Chairman of the Committee on Science and Technology, Environment and Forests, having been authorised by the
 Committee to submit the report on its behalf, present the Eighth Report on the Demands for Grants pertaining to the
 Department of Biotechnology (Ministry of Science and Technology) for the year 1994-95 (Demand No. 73).
2. The Committee held three meetings on March 23, 24 and April 7, 1994 (Annexure). In the meeting held on March 23,
 while considering the Demands for Grants of the Department of Biotechnology, the Committee sought detailed
 clarifications on various development projects, programmes and schemes which fall within the mandate of the
 Department. On its sitting held on March 24, the representatives of the Department replied to the clarifications sought
 by the Hon'ble Members. The Committee wishes to express 'its thanks to the officers of the Department of
 Biotechnology for placing before it the required material and answering the queries-raised by the Hon'ble Members on
 various aspects of the Projects and Programmes administered by the Department to enable it to thoroughly scrutinise,
 the Demands for Grants of the Department of Biotechnology.
3. The Committee considered and adopted the draft report at its meeting held on April 7, 1994

INTRODUCTION
 
I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Science & Technology, Environment
 and Forests, having been authorized by the Committee, present its 154
th Report relating to Wild Life (Protection)
 Amendment *Bill 2005.  The Bill seeks to amend the Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972.
2.         In pursuance of the rules relating to the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committees, Hon’ble
 Chairman, Rajya Sabha **referred the Bill, as introduced in the Rajya Sabha on the 23rd December, 2005 and pending
 therein, to the Committee on the 29th December, 2005 for examination and report within 3 months.
3.         At it first meeting held on the 10th February, 2006, the Committee held internal discussion on the Bill.  At its
 second meeting held on the 21st February 2006, the Committee heard the presentation of the Secretary, Ministry of
 Environment and Forest on the Bill.  In its meetings held on 22nd and 23rd February 2006, it heard the views of the
 Experts on the Bill.  The Committee took clause-by-clause consideration of the Bill on the 1st and 7th March, 2006.
4.         The Committee heard the oral evidence of 3 experts to have better appreciation of the subject.  It also received
 one written submission from one of the experts (Annexure ‘A’).
5.         While considering the Bill, the Committee took note of the following documents/information placed before it:-
(i)         Background note on the Bill received from the Ministry of Environment &      Forests.
(ii)        The Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972.
Report of the Tiger Task Force.
Oral evidence and written submission tendered before the Committee.
Views of the Ministry of Environment & Forests and Ministry of Law & Justice.
6.         The Committee considered and adopted the Report in its meeting held on the 17
th March, 2006.
 7.        For the facility of reference and convenience, the observations and recommendations of the Committee have been
 given in bold letters in the body of the Report.
8.         The Committee expresses its gratitude to the Experts for their valuable suggestions on the Bill. The Committee is
 also thankful to the officials of the Ministry of Environment and Forest and Ministry of Law and Justice for assisting in
 its deliberations.
 
New Delhi P.G. NARAYANAN

The Atomic Energy Commission (AEC), which was set up by a Government of India Resolution on August 10, 1948, is
 the apex body for formulation of policies and direction of the programmes relating to peaceful uses of atomic energy in
 electricity generation, medicine, agriculture, industry and research. The Commission implements its policies and
 programmes that are multidisciplinary in nature through the Department of Atomic Energy (DAE), which was formed on
 August 3, 1954. The Department of Atomic Energy comprises five Research Centres, five Public Sector Undertakings,
 three Industrial Organisations and three service organisations and eight fully funded institutes seven of these institutes are
 engaged in basic research. In addition, the Department’s Board of Research in Nuclear Sciences (BRNS) and the National
 Board for Higher Mathematics (NBHM) promote research in nuclear & allied fields and mathematics.

 the Committee. This Report examines the Annual Report (1993-94) of the Department of Biotechnology with Particular
 reference: to the development of immunodiagnostic kits; environmental conservation and biodiversity; medicinal and
 aromatic plants; and implications of new GATT regime and Intellectual Property Rights (IPRs) with regard to new
 developments in Biotechnology.

            The Ministry of Environment and Fo rests is the nodal agency in the administrative structure o f 
the Central Government for the planning, promotion and coordinati on of environment and forestry
programmes. Within the overall framework of its ma ndate, the main activities of the Ministry include
conservation and survey of flora,  fauna, forests and wildlife, pr evention and control of pollution,
afforestation and regeneration of degraded areas, protection of the environment and ensuring the welfare
of animals. These tasks are sought to be fulf illed through environment impact assessment, eco-
regeneration, assistance to organizations implem enting environmental a nd forestry programmes,
enactment of environmental legi slation, formulation of envir onmental policies, promotion o f
environmental and forestry rese arch, extension, education and tr aining to augment the requisite
manpower, and dissemination of e nvironmental awareness among all sections of the country’s 
population.

INTRODUCTION 
 I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Science & Technology, 
Environment & Forests, having been authorised by th e Committee to present the Report on its behalf, present 
this One Hundred Eighty-first Report on the Action Taken by the Ministry of Earth Sciences on the 
recommendations contained in One Hundred Seventy-third Report of the Committee on Demands for Grants 
(2007-08) of the Ministry of Earth Sciences. 
2. The Report of the Committee deals with the Action Taken by the Ministry of Earth Sciences on the 
recommendations contained in the One Hundred Seventy-third Report of the Department-related Parliamentary 
Standing Committee on Science & Technology, Environment & Forests on the Demands for Grants (2007-08) 
of the Ministry of Earth Sciences which was presented to the Rajya Sabha on 26
th April, 2007. 
3.  There were twenty-three recommendations contained in the One Hundred Seventy-third Report of the 
Committee. Action Taken Notes on the recommendations of the Committee were received from the Ministry 
on 27
th August, 2007. 
4.  In the meeting held on 15 th November, 2007 the Committee considered the draft Action Taken Report and 
adopted the same. 
 
 
 
 
DR. V. MAITREYAN 
NEW DELHI ; Chairman, 
November 15, 2007 Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee 
   on Science and Technology, Environment and Forests.

INTRODUCTION
 
I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Science and Technology, Environment and
 Forests, having been authorised by the Committee to present the Report on its behalf present this Twentieth Report of the
 Committee, This Report deals with three specific areas of activity of the Department of Ocean Development, namely--0)
 Marine Satellite Information Service (MARSIS); (ii) Pollution Monitoring Programme-Coastal Ocean Monitoring and
 Prediction System (COM-PAS) and (iii) National Programme for Identification of Marine Bioactive Substances for use as
 Drugs; on the basis of its Annual Report (1993-94).
 
2. The committee held in all three meetings 6n January 23, 24 and April 27, 1995 to consider the aforementioned
 programmes of the Department. In the meeting held on January 23, 1995 the Secretary of the Department made a presentation
 about the overall activities of the Department, highlighting in particular the thrust being imparted to its programmes in the
 above three areas. On January 24, 1995 the committee further discussed these subjects and the Secretary and other officials of
 the Department of Ocean Development gave clarifications on some of the points raised by the Members.
 
3. The committee thanks the officials of the Department of Ocean Development for giving it-necessary information and
 placing before it relevant papers/background note which facilitated examination of its Annual Report for the year 1993-94.
 
4. The Committee considered and adopted this report at its meeting held on the 27th April, 19.95.

REPORT
The Ministry of Environment and Forests is the nodal agency at the national level for planning, promotion and co-ordination of
 environmental and forestry programmes . Its mandate includes survey and conservation of flora, fauna, forests and wildlife; prevention and
 control of pollution; afforestation and regeneration of degraded areas; and in general protection of the environment. Pursuant to this mandate,
 the tasks undertaken by the Ministry are: environmental impact assessment; eco-regeneration; assistance to organisations implementing
 environmental and forestry programs; enactment of environmental legislation; formulation of environmental policies; promotion of
 environmental and forestry . research, extension, education and training to augment the requisite manpower; dissemination of environmental
 information, creation of environmental awareness among all sections of the country's population; and international cooperation.
2. A total outlay of Rs. 435.41 crores for the year 1995-96 has been proposed, vide demand no. 22 for the Ministry of Environment and
 Forests to enable it to fulfill its mandate. The Plan component of this outlay is Rs. 370.50 crores and the Non-Plan component Rs. 64.91
 crores. The allocations for the year 1995-96 represent an increase of Rs. 10.50 crores in the Plan Sector and about Rs. 5 crores in the Non-
Plan Sector over the revised estimates for the year 1994-95. In terms of activity-wise allocations, the Plan allocations for forestry and wildlife
 have gone up from Rs. 203.09 crores to Rs 210.15 cr

and Technology, Environment and Forests, having been authorized by the Committee to present the
Report on its behalf, present this Two Hundred Thirtieth Report on Steps Taken by various sectors
of the Indian Economy to Control Pollution.
2. The Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Science and Technology,
Environment and Forests, decided to take up for consideration the subject ‘Steps Taken by various
sectors of the Indian Economy to Control Pollution’ and report thereon.
3. In this regard the Committee heard the views of the Secretaries, Ministries/Departments of
Environment and Forests, Coal, Mines, Steel, Power, Petroleum and Natural Gas, Heavy Industry,
Shipping (including Ports), Railways, Civil Aviation, Road Transport and Highways, Defence,
Defence Production, Health and Family Welfare, Agriculture, Urban Development, Chemicals and
Fertilizers (D/o Pharmaceuticals) and Tourism. The Committee, in all held 14 meetings and devoted
33.51 hours in the process of the consideration of the subject. The Committee also visited Mumbai,
Goa, Bengaluru, Visakhapatnam to get first hand information on the State of Pollution and measures
taken to mitigate it.

INTRODUCTION
I, the Chairman of the Committee on Science and Technology, Environment and Forests, having been, authorised
 by the Committee to submit the Report on its behalf, present this Twenty Fifth Report, on the Demands for Grants
 pertaining to the Department of Electronics for the year 1995-96 (Demand No. 87).

 the other representatives of the Department.
3. The Committee thanks the officers of the Department for providing necessary information to the Hon'ble
 Members to facilitate consideration of its Demands for Grants.
4. The Committee considered and adopted the Report at its meeting held on May 10, 1995.
 
 
NEW DELHI SYED SIBTEY RAZI
May 10, 1995 Chairman

 production in the electronics sector bas shown a faster growth state than achieved in any other industrial sector. The
 Department of Electronics has been vested with the responsibility of formulation, implementation and review of
 national policies in the field of electronics. The other tasks of the Department include development of appropriate new
 technologies through R&D programmes, promoting applications of electronics particularly export oriented, creation of
 infrastructure for standardisation , testing and quality certification, development of manpower resources and co-
ordination of various applications of electronics.

having been authorised by the Committee to submit the report on its behalf, present the Thirty­
first Report, on the Demands for Grants pertaining to the Department of Science and

Grants of the Department of Science and Technology on the basis of documents made available 
to it and the submissions made before it by the Secretary and other officials of the Department.

sought by the Hon 'ble Members and placing before it the required material to enable the 
Committee to scrutinise the Demands for Grants of the Department of Science and Technology.

1996. 
5. In pursuance of the national objective of making scientific and technological progress 
and attaining self-reliance, Department of Science and Technology (DST) has been assigned 
nodal responsibilities for coordinating research and development in frontier areas of science and 
technology. Over the years the departments and autonomous institutions under Department of 
Science and Technology have been making consistent efforts to foster research and 
development (R & D) activities, resulting in development of infrastructure in diverse fields of 
Science & Technology, administration, human resource, etc. The department lays emphasis on 
planning process which emanates from the Panchayat Level through its Meteorology and Survey 
Departments. 
6. The Secretary, Department of Science and Technology, in his presentation before the 
Committee, gave an overview of the thrust areas, which the Department intended to take up 
during the year 1996-97, for which allocations were made in the Budget for the year 1996-97 for

I, the Chairman of the Committee on Science & Technology, Environment & Forests, 
having been authorised by the Committee to submit the Report on its behalf, present this 
32nd Report on the Demands for Grants pertaining to the Department of Electronics for the 
year 1996-97. 
2. The Committee held in all one meeting on August 13, 1996. In the meeting held on 
13th August, 1996 while deliberating on the Demands for Grants of the Department of 
Electronics, the Committee sought detailed clarifications and explanations from the 
representatives of the Department of Electronics. The Committee wishes to express its 
thanks to the officers of the Department of Electronics and the Planning Commission for 
placing before it the requisite material and answering the queries raised by Members on 
various aspects of the Electronics programme and related aspects to enable it to scrutinise 
the Demands for Grants . 
3. The Committee considered and adopted its draft report at its meeting held on 23rd 
August, 1996. 
4. Electronics, in one form or the other, is the backbone of the entire industrial activity. 
Department of Electronics (DOE) is the promotional department of Government of India 
committed to development of Indian industry and applications of IT and electronics in the 
general walk of life in India. DOE is committed to development of technology tools and 
applications and in geheral to the proper utilisation of technology in society in public. DOE 
does technology forecasting exercise in which technology plays profound impact on society 
and people. Computer networking was one such area identified 10 years ago by DOE before 
it was perceived by other agencies in the country. In a similar approach DOE initiated a 
programme calle.d ERNET to fo~s on development of national capability in computer 
network in the country. It has led to the movement similar to Internet which was infact not 
known in those days. DOE has played a pioneer role in publidsing E-Mail and subsequently 
providing it in the country. 
5. While DOE is the promotional agency for electronics in the country, Department of 
Telecommunications (DOT) is the nodal agency in the field of telecommunications and it has 
played a big role in the development of telecommunications in the country. As such DOT 
and DOE are complimentary agencies in furthering the total area on IT, electronics and 
telecommunications. Therefore, the two agencies have to work together to converge at the 
technology level in telecommunications and IT electronics. 
6. DOE has ~hree public sector undertakings namely CMC, ET &T and SCL. Besides, a 
large number of societies including C-DAC, ER&DC, STPI, SAMEER, CEDT , DOEACC, 
NCST. DOE also has a large outfit of STQC laboratories all over the country. These 
agencies act as the anns of the Department in fulfilling its goals.

             INTRODUCTION  
 
  I, the Chairman of the Department -related Parliamentary Standing Committee on 
Science and Technology, Environment, Forests and Climate Change , having been authorised by 
the Committee to present the Report on its behalf, present this Three Hundred Twenty Sixth 
Report of the Committee.  This Report deals with the d etailed Demands for Grants (2020-2021) 
of the Department of Atomic Energy (Demand No.3). 
 
2.   In the meeting of the Committee held on the 18th February, 2020, the Secretary and 
other officers of the Department of Atomic Energy gave an overview of the various activities of 
the Department and the Members sought clarifications on various aspects of the performance of 
the Department to enable it to scrutinise the Demands for Grants. 
  
3.   The Committee expresses its thanks to the officers of the Department for replying to the
