having been authorised by the Committee to submit the Report on its behalf , present this 
33rd Report on the Demands for Grants pertaining to the Department of Space ft. r the year 
1996-97 (Demand No. 91). 
2. The Committee held in aJI one meeting on August 9, 1996. In the meeting held on 
August 9, 1996, while deliberating on the Demands for Grants of the Department of Space, 
the Committee sought detailed clarifications and explanations from the representatives of the 
Departm ent of Space. The Committee wishes to express its thanks to the officers of the 
Department of Space for placing before it the requisite material and answering the queries 
raised by Members on various aspects of the Space Programme and related aspects to enable 
it to scrutinise the Demands for Grants.

23, 1996. 
4. The Indian Space Programme assumes significance in the context of advances made 
in the space technology and its varied applications in the field of national development on a 
sustainable basis in key areas like communication, meteorology, natural resources 
management and environmental monitoring, in a timely, cost effective and self-reliant 
manner. Remarkable developments in space technology and its application have thus 
contributed significantly towards utilization of our natural resources. 
5. The setting up of the Thumba Equatorial Rocket Launching Station (TERLS) in 
early sixties marked the beginning of the Indian Space Programme. The Space Commission 
and the Department of Space were established by the Government in 1972 with a view to 
promote unified development and application of space science and technology for identified 
national objectives. Many advanced countries, which pursued Space programme~ since 1950s, 
were motivated by the desire to be at the forefront of exploration and Science to stay at the 
cutting edge of technology in aerospace, to establish human presence in space and to exploit 
commercially the benefits that accrued from these efforts . It is because space provides 
advantage point to view the planet Earth in its totality and to facilitate connectivity, cutting 
across physical barriers and trans nat_ional boundaries. 
6. The thrust of our Space Programme is towards the goal of self-reliant use of space

REPORT 
1, the Chairman of the Committee on Science and Technology, Environment and 
Forests, having been authorised by the Committee to submit the report on its behalf, present 
this 34th Report of the Committee. This Report deals with the Demands for Grants 
pertaining to Department of Biotechnology (Ministry of Science & Technology) for the year 
1996-97 (Demand No. 76). 
2. In the meeting of the Committee held on the 13th August, 1996, the representatives 
of the Department of Biotechnology gave an overview of the various activities of the 
Department and the Committee sought clarifications on the various aspects of the 
functioning of the Department of Biotechnology. 
3. The Committee wishes to express its thanks to the officers of the Department of 
Biotechnology for their cooperation and answering the queries raised by Hon'ble Members 
on various aspects on programmes initiated by the Department. 
4~ The Committee considered and adopted the draft report at its meeting held on the 
23rd August, 1996. 
5. The world has witnessed spectacular advances in the field of biotechnology in the last 
43 years after the Nobel Prize discovery of the structure and D~A by Watson and Crick, in 
1993. The field was regarded as the greatest individual enterprise of the humankind in this 
century. It has revolutionised the industrial scenario, specially, the pharmaceutical industry 
all over the world, in particular, in advanced countries. Biotechnology is a science which 
uses the living organisms to make or modify a product-to improve plants or animals and 
microorganisms for specific uses. It aims at harnessing the genetic diversity in the living 
organisms for manufacture of useful products and production of strains of microbes, plants 
and animals with improved qualities. 
6. The need to accelerate the pace of research in biotechnology was felt in India.

REPORT 
I, the Chairman of the Committee on Science and Technology, Environment & Forests 
having been authorised by the Committee to present the report on its behalf, present the 
Thirty-sixth Report, on the Demands for Grants pertaining to the Department of Scientific 
and Industrial Research for the year 1996-97 (Demand No. 75). 
2. In its meetings held on 13th and 22nd August, 1996 the Committee discussed in detail 
the Demands for Grants of the Department of Scientific and Industrial Research on the 
basis of documents made av·ailable to it and the submissions made before it by the Secretary 
of the Department and the other representatives of the Department. 
3. The Committee expresses its thanks to the officers of the Department for replying to 
the clarifications sought by the Hon'ble Members and placing before it the required material 
to enable the Committee to scrutinise the Demands for Grants of the Department of 
Scientific and Industrial Research. 
4. The Committee considered and adopted the Report at its meeting held on 
September 3, 1996. 
5. The thrust of the programmes and activities of the Department of Scientific and 
Industrial Research (DSIR) is on the activities of Council of Scientific and Industrial 
Research (CSIR)- a premier Science and Technology (S&T) agency with a network of 40 
national laboratories, two complexes and 81 Extension and Regional Centres spread all over 
the country, Technology Promotion, Development, Utilisation and Transfer (TPDU) and 
National Information System for Science and Technology (NISSAT). 
6. Other major programmes of the Department include Research and Development by 
Industry (RDI) consisting of in-house R & D in Industry, Scientific and Industrial Research 
Organisations (SIROs) and Fiscal ·Incentives for Scientific Research; Programme Aimed at 
Technological Self Reliance {PATSER) consisting of development of new or improved 
technologies. Development of speciaVcustom built capital goods, absorption and adaptation 
of improved technology, studies and interactions concerning Technology Evaluation and pre­
feasibility reports of major sectors/products; Scheme to Enhance the Efficacy of Transfer of 
Technology (SEETOT) consisting of National Register of Foreign Collaborations (NRFC), 
Industrial Technology, Transfer and Trading in Technology (TA TT), Linkages with 
International Organisations including Asian and Pacific Centres for Transfer of Technology 
(APCIT) and Promotion and Support to Consultancy Services (PSCS) including the 
Consultancy Development Centre (CDC) and two Public Enterprises viz. National Research 
Development Corporation (NRDC) and Central Electronics Limited (CEL) engaged in the 
commercialisation of indigeneously developed technologies.

1, the Chairman of the Committee on Science and Technology, Environment and 
Forests, having been authorised by the Committee to present the report on its behalf. 
present the Thirty-seventh Report, on the Demands for Grants pertaining to the Ministry of 
Environment and Forests for the year 1996-97 (Demand No. 22). 
2. In its meeting held on 8th and 22nd August, 1996 the Committee discussed in detail 
the Demands for Grants of the Ministry of Environment and Forests on the basis of 
documents made available and the submissions made before it by the Secretary and other 
officials of the Department. 
3. The Committee thanks the officers of the Ministry for replying to the clarifications 
sought by the Hon'ble Members and placing before it the required material to enable the 
Committee to scrutinise the Demands for Grants of the Ministry of Environment and 
Forests . 
4. The Committee considered and adopted the Report at its meeting held on 9th 
September , 1996. 
5. India , the seventh largest country (area 329 million ha.) in the world, covers 2% of 
land area, while supporting 16% of human population (900 million) and 15% of cattle 
population (480 million): It is one of the 12 mega bio-diversity countries, commanding 7% 
of the world bio-diversity. India has merely 1% of forest area and 112% of grazing land of 
the world. Per capita forest area in the country works out to 0.08 ha. as against global 
average of about 1.00 ha. Forests in the country are thus subjected to enormous biotic 
pressures. 
6. The very existence of the country and its all-round progress is greatly dependent on 
sustainable development. lt is, therefore, vital 'that a check is exercised on the environment . 
Our hoary traditions of environmental conservation which have inculcated in us a deep 
reverence for nature and an awareness of the age-old truth that all forms of life, be it 
human, animal or plant are inter-woven and any damage to one may cause serious threat to 
the rest. The age-old traditions of environment protection and reverence to the mother 
nature have been given prominence in our national priorities. It is therefore duty of 
everyone of us to protect and improve the natural environment, including forest, lakes, 
rivers and wildlife and to have compassion for living creatures. However, it is being noticed 
that as a result of economic progress pressure is steadily increasing on the environment and 
the natural resources. 
7. Over the years , the countries have realised the importance of protecting environment 
and preserving forests for the welfare and good of the mankind . The organisation of the 
Stockholm Conference on Environment and Development in 1972 further provided impetus 
to this realisation amongst the countries, whether developed or developing. In India, the 
Departm ent of Environment, as a separate department, was set up towards the end of 1980.

I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on 
Science and Technology, Environment and Forests, having been authorised by the 
Committee, do hereby present on its behalf, this 40th Report of the Committee. This 
report deals with the programmes and functioning of the Department of Bio-technology 
with special emph asis on the role of Bio-technology in Agriculture and Allied areas on the 
basis of 'Mid- Term Appraisal' undertaken by the Committee. 
2. In the meeting of the Committee held on the 27th January, 1997, the Secretary and 
other officers of the Department of Bio-technology gave an overview of the various 
activities of the Department and the Committee sought clarifications on the various aspects 
of the functioning of the Department particularly about the activities relating to the fields 
of Crop Biotechnology , Biofertilizer, Biopesticides , Sericulture, Plant Tissue Culture, 
Acquaculture, Biosafet y, financial aspects, etc. 
3. The Committee wishes to express its appreciation to the officers of the Department 
of Biotechnology for their coo peration and making available the material requisitioned by 
the Committee on various aspects on programmes undertaken by the Department. 
4. The Committee conside red and adopted the draft report at its meeting held on the 
5th March, 1997.

1953, major breakthroughs have taken place in the field of Mole cular Biology lead ing to a

  INTRODUCTION 
 
 
          I,  the  Chairman of the Department -related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Science 
and Technology, Environment, Forests and Climate Change, having been authorized by the 
Committee to present the Report on its behalf, present this Four Hundred Fourth Report on  
“Review of the functioning of Tata Memorial Centre (TMC), Bhabha Atomic Research Centre 
(BARC) and Nuclear Power Corporation of India Limited (NPCIL)”. 
2.   Tata Memorial Centre (TMC) is a grant -in-aid institute under the Department of Atomic 
Energy (DAE). It serves approximately 150,000 new cancer patients annually, making it one of 
India‟s largest and most advanced cancer care institutions. The Committee visited TMC on 21 st 
September, 2025 as part of its study tour to Chandigarh and Mumbai from 19th to 2 2nd September 
2025 to explore the remarkable contributions being made by the institute in the field of cancer 
research and treatment, and to discuss the challenges and opportunities that lie ahead in advancing 
India‟s capabilities in these critical areas. 
3.  Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (BARC) is an R&D institution under the Department of 
Atomic Energy. Nuclear Power Corporation of India Limited (NPCIL) is a Public Sector Enterprise 
under the administrative control of the  Department of Atomic Energy (DAE) , responsible for 
design, construction, commissioning and operation of nuclear power reactors. The Committee 
visited BARC on 21 st September 2025 as part of its study tour to Chandigarh and Mumbai from 
19th to 22nd September 2025 to gain first -hand information about various aspects such as progress 
and roadmap of India‟s three-stage nuclear power programme, advancements in indigenous reactor 
technology, including Small Modular Reactors (SMRs) and the pivotal thorium cycle, the critical

this Fifty-first Report of the Committee. This Report deals with the Demands for Grants 
pertaining to Department of Biotechnology (Ministry of Science & Technology) for the year

2. In the meeting of the Committee held on the 15th April, 1997, the representatives of 
the Department of Biotechnology gave an overview of the. various activities of the 
Department and the Committee sought clarification on the various aspects of the functioning

4. The world has witnessed spectacular advances in the fields of biotechnology during 
the last 44 years after the discovery of the structure and DNA by Watson and Crick, in 
1953, for which they were awarded Nobel Prize in Medicines and Physiology. The field was 
regarded as the greatest individual enterprise of the humankind. It has revolutionised the 
industrial scenario, especially, the pharmaceutical industry all over the world, particularly in 
technologically advanced countries. Biotechnology is a science which uses the living 
organisms to make or modify a product-to improve plants or animals and microorganisms for 
specific uses. It aims at harnessing the genetic diversity in the living organisms for 
manufacture of useful products and production of strains of microbes, plants and animals 
with improved qualities. 
5. The Department of Biotechnology, estabished in 1986, is expected to give a greater 
impetus to the development of biotechnology in the country. The objectives of the 
Department include development of products and processes and technologies whose large­
scale applications would result in societal and economic benefits.

authorised by the Committee to present the report on its behalf, present this Fifty-Ninth Report of the Committee.

The Indian Space Programme, which had a modest beginning in the early sixt ies, is primarily aimed at 
promoti ng the development and application of space technology and space sciences for the socio-economic ben­
efits of the nation. Over the last three decades, the very challenging task of development of space technology and 
its utilisation, has not only graduated from establishment and expe rimental phase s to an operational era but also 
proved emphatically its potential to address the national needs. 
2. In tune with the goal of self-reliant use of space technology for national development, the main thrust

67th Report on Demands for Grants of Department of Electronics
 
The Department of Electronics (DOE)  is responsible for the development of the electronics industry formulation,
 promoting application  of electronics and informative technology,  implementation and review of various programmes/schemes
 in the field of electronics.  These schemes are implemented both in-house as well as through PSUs /Societies  under DOE and
 also through various sponsored programmes being funded under R&D.
2.         The Department is a medium not only to provide a focal point of Government’s attention to electronics sector and also to
 function as a coordinator within and outside the Government, but is also responsible for bringing the benefits of electronics to
 every walk of life, and play a catalytic role to make the Indian Electronics Industry a global player  in the light of the new
 Industrial and Trade Policy.
3.         With delicensing of the entire electronics industry (except aerospace and defence electronics), liberalisation in foreign
 investment and Export-Import policies, the country is witnessing new investments, restructuring of existing activities,
 diversification of the product range and an intensely  competitive environment.  All the renowned global brands have either
 established production facilities in the country or are present in the market through technical/financial collaborations, thus
 giving consumer a wider choice in terms of product features, technology quality and competitive prices.
4.         The thrust , according to  DOE, during the Ninth Plan, would be on Export, Employment and productivity-led growth of
 Electronics and Information Technology.  The electronics and Information Technology sector has the propensity to increase the
 overall growth rate to higher level.
5.            Electronics is the fast growing sector of the Indian industry.  During the Eighth Plan, the electronics industry had a
 cumulative annual growth of 20 per cent in production and over 40 per cent in exports.  The electronics industry achieved a
 production level of Rs. 32,070 crores and an export performance of Rs. 9, 500 crores during the year 1997-98 and is likely to
 achieve a production level of Rs. 41,000 crores during the year 1998-99 registering a growth of over 28% and export
 performance of Rs.12800/- showing a net increase of 70 per cent.  A goal of annual electronics production of Rs. 1,38,350
 crores and exports of about Rs. 49,000 crores has been set for the terminal year of the Ninth Plan (2001-02), representing a
 growth rate of 39% and 52% respectively.
BUDGETARY ALLOCATION
6.         The Department was given an allocation of Rs. 791.78 for the entire 8
th Five Year Plan, out of which budgetary support
 was to the tune of Rs.  679.38 crores .  An allocation of Rs. 897.37 crores has been made available for the 9 th Five Year Plan
 (1997-2002) and Gross Budgetary support would be pegged at Rs. 542.37 crores.  .  During the first three years of plan Rs.
 769.57 crores  have been spent and left over allocation  is only Rs. 127.8 crores and the share of Budgetary support spent so far
 is Rs. 405.6 crores leaving a balance of Rs. 136.77 cores (Appendix –I).
 
 
7.            Budgetary support for the Department of Electronics for the current financial  year  is Rs. 208 crores (Rs. 180 crores
 Plan and Rs. 28 crores Non-Plan) against the revised estimate 1998-99 of Rs. 156.57 crores (Rs. 135 crores Plan and Rs. 21.57
 crores Non-Plan)(See Appendix –II).  The allocation for the year is thus Rs. 51.43 crores more than RE 1998-99.
8.         As regards the justification for  enhanced allocation the Committee was informed an enhanced outlay of Rs. 20 crores
 has been provided  for setting up of  an  IT Venture Capital Fund .  Besides, an amount of  Rs. 5.00 crores are likely to be spent

Sixty-Eighth   Report on Demands for Grants (1999-2000)
of the Department of Space
 
            India’s Space Programme, since its inception in the early sixties, has been guided by a vision which laid emphasis on the
 application of space technology for finding solution to the problems of man and society thereby establishing a viable & self
 reliant space programme.  From the very beginning, long-range plans have been drawn up to steer the programme effectively
 ensuring appropriate linkages among the application needs, satellite missions, launch vehicle capabilities and technology
 development.  Over the last three-and-half decades, significant progress has been made  in  space technology for building
 world-class satellites for communications and remote sensing; for launching the remote sensing satellites from India with
 indigenous launch vehicle; and providing the benefits of space technology to improve the quality of life at the grass root level,
 thus contributing to several areas of national development.
2.         In tune with the goal of self reliant use of space technology for national development, the thrust areas of the Indian
 Space Programme include:-
(a)        satellite  based communication for various applications.
(b)        satellite based remote sensing for resources survey, management and environmental monitoring;
(c)        meteorological applications; and
(d)        development and operationalisation of indigenous and launch vehicles for providing these space services.
3.         The Department of Space (DOS) is responsible for implementing the policies framed by the Space Commission.  The
 policies are carried out through the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) and the three Grant in aid institutions, viz. the
 National Remote Sensing Agency (NRSA), the Physical Research Laboratory (PRL) and the National Mesosphere-
Stratosphere-Troposphere Radar Facility (NMRF).
4.         The cumulative expenditure on space research till the end of Eighth Plan period i.e. from the inception in 1962-63 to
 1996-97, is Rs.7431.67 crore.  During the Eighth Plan, most of the programmatic targets and missions planned have been
 achieved. The total expenditure incurred is Rs.3928.53 crore (Plan Rs.3155.74 crore and Non-Plan Rs.772.79 crore). The major
 missions achieved are INSAT-2B, INSAT-2C, INSAT-2D, IRS-1E, IRS-P2, IRS-1C, IRS-P3, SROSS-C1 and SROSS-C2.
 Besides, considerable progress in the areas like development of indigenous cryogenic engine and stage for the GSLV
 programme, technological development for indigenisation of strategic and critical sub-systems & components and setting up of
 facilities for realisation of inertial systems and electro-optical systems have been achieved. 
5.         The Committee was informed that the Planning Commission has allocated a Plan outlay of Rs.6511.72 crore, against
 their earlier communication of Rs.7100.00 crore and the Non-Plan outlay of Rs.1200 crore for the Ninth Plan period. Thus, the
 total outlay for the Ninth Plan is Rs.7711.72 crore. However, the actual Plan budgetary allocation would be decided annually
 based on the programmatic requirements.
6.         The programme directions and the programmatic targets for the Ninth Plan have been formulated after extensive
 interactions and consultations with user Ministries. The major missions planned for the Ninth Plan to realise the programmatic
 targets have been indicated in Annexure-I. While the basic vision would continue to be the large scale application of space
 technology for finding solutions to the problems of man and society, the programme would respond effectively to the dynamic
 and complex problems of the coming years. The   major programmes planned include (i) operationalisation of Geosynchronous
 Satellite Launch Vehicle (GSLV) towards achievement of self-reliance in launching communication satellites;  (ii) providing
 additional and newer operational communication satellite services to meet the increasing national needs;  (iii) building earth
 observation systems for wide range of applications related to land, water and ocean resources as well as atmospheric
 observations; (iv) establishing the GRAMSAT programme for integrating the potentials of satellite communication and remote
 sensing for rural development including the tele-education and tele-health; (v) establishing new communication services for
 Digital Audio and Data Broadcasting and Direct to Home TV services; (vi) establishing a viable system for Disaster
 Management through Earth observation, satellite-based communications, conventional survey information and local networks;
 (vii) research and development as well as technology development; and (viii) enhanced interface between Indian industry and
 academia to give boost to the national space ef

69th Report on Demands for Grants (1999-2000)of the Department
of Scientific and Industrial Research
 
The Department of Scientific and Industrial Research which forms a part of the Ministry of Science and Technology
 comprises of activities of Departmental Schemes viz. Research and Development by Industry (RDI), Programme
 Aimed at Technological Self Reliance (PASTER), Scheme to Enhance the Efficacy of Transfer of Technology
 (SEETOT), National Information System for Science and Technology (NISSAT) and management of the public sector
 undertaking, National Research Development Corporation (NRDC) and Central Electronics Limited (CEL). The long
 term objective of the programme on Research by Industry and Technology Transfer is technological self-reliance and
 the short term objectives are promotion of R&D by Industry and enhancing efficacy of technology transfer, both
 domestic and foreign. Issues addressed in these programmes include identification of technological gaps, making
 investment in R&D by Industry attractive and productive, development and commercialisation of domestic
 technologies through. In – house R&D in industry and R&D by public funded laboratories coupled with industry. The
 Department also looks after matters concerning the Council of Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR) which
 functions as a registered society and has a network of 40 laboratories and 81 field stations/extension centres/regional
 centres located all over the country that undertake R&D in various science and technology areas and disciplines.
2. The Secretary explained the achievements of the National Laboratories under the CSIR, in the fields of Aerospace,
 Biology and Biotechnology, Chemicals, Drugs and Pharmaceuticals, Earth resources and Natural hazards mitigation,
 Ecology and Environment, Food and Food Processing etc. which have tangible impact on the socio-economy sectors,
 during the Eighth Five Year Plan and informed about the new projects which the Department proposes to undertake
 during the year 1999-2000.
3. The Secretary also gave a brief presentation on the recent earthquake having an epicentre in the Chamoli region of
 Uttar Pradesh. The Committee enquired about the efforts made by the Department to arrest the damage and
 rehabilitation plans. The Committee specifically wanted to know whether any lead has been made for scientifically
 predicting earthquake. The Committee was informed that within CSIR a National Geophysical research Institute,
 Hyderabad and Central building Research Institute, Roorke are working for minimising the damage after an earthquake.
 As regards, predicting earthquakes, it was stated that as of today, there is no scientifically accepted method available to
 predict earthquakes accurately enough to be of help in saving human lives as there are no well established precursors
 which precede earthquake. A member pointed out that such an event in China was once preceded by strange behaviour
 of animals which led an elder to forecast that an earthquake was about to come and city was got vacated which helped
 minimise the damage. However, it is possible today to broadly work out the earthquake hazard in terms of accelerations
 that may occur at a given region based on the previous earthquake records. Then, on the basis of local geology and
 several other factors, it is possible to carry out mico zoning which indicates the kind of acceleration that would be
 expected in areas at a scale of a few hectares to a few square kilometres. Thereafter retrofitting of vulnerable structures
 can be done to save non engineered structures.
BUDGETARY ALLOCATIONS
4. The financial allocation for the Department of Scientific and Industrial Research for the year 1999-2000 is Rs.820.46
 crores as against Rs.737.46 crores in the R.E. of 1998-99 and Rs.638.00 crores in the B. E. of 1998-99 . Thus represents
 an increase in Rs.83.00 crores over the revised estimates and Rs.182.46 crores over the B.E. of 1998-99.(ANNEXURE
 )

70th Report on Demands for Grants (1999-2000)
of the  Ministry of Environment and Forests
 
 
            The mandate of the Ministry of Environment and Forests extends to planning, promotion and co-ordination of environmental
 and forestry programmes.  The main activities of the Ministry relate to conservation and control of pollution, survey of flora, fauna,
 forests and wildlife, afforestation, and re-generation of degraded areas, protection of environment and research concerning these
 subjects. The Ministry discharges its mandate through environmental impact assessment, eco-regeneration; assistance to organisations
 implementing environmental and forestry research programmes; enactment of environmental legislation; formulation of
 environmental policies; promotion of environmental and forestry research, extension, education and training to augment the requisite

REPORT
The Chairman, Rajya Sabha in pursuance of the rules relating to the Department-related Parliamentary Standing
 Committees, referred* the Semiconductor Integrated Circuits Layout-Design Bill, 1999, as introduced in the Rajya
 Sabha on the 20 th December, 1999, and pending therein, to the Committee for examination and Report by the 15 th
 February, 2000.
2. The above reference was considered by the Committee in its meetings held on 8 th February, 2000. After some
 discussion the Committee felt that it would not be possible for it to complete the examination of the provisions of the
 Semiconductor Integrated Circuits Layout Bill-1999 ** and submit its report within the stipulated time i.e.15th
 February, 2000. Accordingly, Chairman, Rajya Sabha was requested to grant extension of time to the Committee, upto
 the 29th day of February, 2000, for presentation of its report on the Bill. The request for extension of time was granted
 and notified in the Rajya Sabha Bulletin Part II dated the 23rd February,2000.
3. Electronics and Information Technology is one of the fastest growing sectors that has played a significant role in the
 world economy. This was primarily due to the advancement in the filed of electronics, computers and
 telecommunications. Microelectronics has rightly been recognized as a core strategic technology world over, especially
 for the Information Technology (IT) based society. Design of Integrated Circuit (IC) required considerable expertise
 and several hundreds of man-years of effort depending on the complexity. Such efforts culminate into the layouts for
 ICs, which are used for fabricating the ICs in the fabrication plants. In order to encourage continued investment in
 R&D leading to technological advancements in the field of microelectronics, protection of Intellectual Property Rights
 is of utmost importance.
4. The question regarding the type of the protection to be given to the layout design of Integrated Circuits is relatively
 new. Although prefabricated components of electrical circuitry have been used for a long time in the manufacture of
 electrical equipment (for example radios) large scale integration of a multitude of electrical functions in a very small
 component became possible only a few years ago as a result of advances in Semiconductor Technology. Integrated
 Circuits are manufactured in accordance with very detailed plans or "Layout designs".
transistors were fabricated and packaged separately and then connected on a board to realise on electrical circuit. With
 the advances in microelectronics technology, it has become possible to
______________________________________________________________________________
* Rajya Sabha Parliamentary Bulletin Part II, dated the 21st January, 2000.
** Annexure.
integrate several such devices on a small chip of semiconducting material. Such circuits are, therefore, called Integrated
 Circuits (ICs).
5. "Integrated Circuit" means a product in its final form or an intermediate form, in which the elements, at least one of
 which is an active element, and some or all of one of the connections are integrally formed in and which is intended to
 perform on electronic function.
"Layout Design" means the three – dimensional disposition, at least one
of which is an active element and of some or all of the interconnections of an integrated circuit, or such a three
 dimensional disposition prepared for an integrated circuit is intended for manufacture.
6. A layout-design of integrated circuit is a creation of human mind. It is the result of an enormous investment, both in
 terms of time of highly qualified experts and financial investment. There is a continuing need for the creation of new
 layout-designs which reduce the dimensions of existing integrated circuits and simultaneously increase their functions.

REPORT 71

 The smaller an integrated circuit, the less is the material needed for its manufacture, and smaller is the space needed to
 accommodate it. Integrated Circuits are utilized in a large range of products, including articles of mass consumption,
 such as watches, television sets, washing machines, automobiles, etc., as well as sophisticated data processing
 equipment.
Whereas the creation of a new layout-design for an integrated circuit involves an
important investment, the copying of such a layout design may cost only a fraction of that investment. Copying may be
 done by photographing each layer of an integrated circuit and preparing masks for the protection of the integrated
 circuit on the basis of the photographs obtained. The possibility of such copying is the main reason for the introduction
 of legislation for the protection of layout designs.

R E P O R T
 
 The mandate of the Ministry of Environment and Forests entails planning, promotion and coordination of environment
 and forestry programmes. The main activities of the Ministry relate to conservation and control of pollution,
 afforestation and regeneration of forests in degraded areas, protection and conservation of forests, wildlife and
 protection of environment. The tasks are sought to be achieved through environmental impact assessment, eco-
regeneration, assistance to organisations implementing environmental and forestry programmes, enactment of
 environmental legislation, formulation of environmental policies, promotion of environmental and forestry research,
 extension, education and training to augment the requisite manpower, dissemination of environmental awareness
 among all sectors of the country’s population. The activities of the Ministry are divided in four major sectors, i.e.
1. Environment,
2. National River Conservation Directorate,
3. Forests and Wildlife and
4. National Afforestation and Eco-Development Board.
 
NINTH PLAN AND ANNUAL PLANS
2. The total central sector ninth plan (1997-2002) allocation is Rs.489361.58 crores. Out of this, the share of Ministry of
 Environment and Forests is only Rs.3013.84 crores, i.e. only 0.61% of the total central plan outlay. The actual
 expenditure of the Ministry in 1998-99 was Rs.498.05 crores against the revised estimate of rs.468.00 crores. An
 allocation of Rs.7000.00 crores was made for 1999-2000. It was revised by the Ministry of Finance to Rs.610 crores at
 R.E. stage, Ministry is expected to spend Rs.610.00 crores during 1999-2000 which is 22.48% higher then 1998-99.

79th Report on the Information Technology Bill, 1999
 
 The Chairman, Rajya Sabha in pursuance of the rules relating to the Department-related Parliamentary Standing
 Committees, referred* the Information Technology Bill, 1999**, as introduced in the Lok Sabha on 16 th December,
 1999 and pending therein, to the Standing Committee on Science & Technology, Environment & Forests for
 examination and Report.
2. In the present day world it has been the electronics and now the Information Technology (IT) which influence our life
 the most. There is hardly any area of human endeavour where electronic gadgets have not reached. There is barely any
 industry which does not depend, for its efficiency and productivity, on the application of electronics in its different
 manifestations. Technology has emerged as the vehicle of rapid change in the work culture and the way mankind
 communicates in the century. India has been no exception to this phenomenon. Whether in the field of
 telecommunications, roads, ports or air travel, the hallmark has been more efficient and cost effective technology. Thus
 from slow-moving majestic automobiles the country has moved to smart and fast technologies which have given us
 much more advanced vehicles, coal guzzling steam locomotives which have been replaced by electric traction engines.
3. Information Technology is a product of information age and technology. It is a vehicle for future development,
 opportunities, challenges and competition that enables faster collection and dissemination of information. In the history
 of civilization, no work of science has had so comprehensive an impact on human development as IT. Undoubtedly, IT
 has been the greatest changing agent of this century and promises to play its role even more dramatically in the times to
 come. IT is changing every aspect of human life, breaking old barriers and building new inter connections in the
 emerging global village and becoming the chief determinant of progress of nations and that of individuals. IT is being
 meaningfully employed in railways and airlines, banking, insurance, weather forecasting, radio astronomy, molecular
 biology, aerodynamics, etc. thereby reducing the fatigue and increasing the productivity and efficiency. And in
 education too, IT has a vital role. A large variety of software is available to cater to self-learning and evaluation on
 various subjects.
4. IT is a broad term covering the entire gamut of managing and processing information. Computer hardware, software
 and internet are the tools for the systems that have been designed, developed, supported or managed by IT
 professionals. The discovery of computers and subsequent development of the technology popularly known as
 information technology is one of the most significant achievements of the 20
th century. The role of IT as an instrument
 for progress and development has been acknowledged widely and is expected to bring in major social and economic
 benefits for the mankind and accelerate the process of development.

th January, 2000

INTRODUCTION 
 
I, the Chairperson, Standing Committee on Social Justice and 
Empowerment (2020-21) having been authorized by the Committee to submit the 
Report on their behalf, do present this Fifteenth Report on the action taken by the 
Government on the observations/recommendations contained in the Sixth Report 
of the Standing Committee on Social Justice and Empowerment (Seventeenth 
Lok Sabha) on 'Demands for Grants (2020 -21)' of the Ministry of Social Justice 
and Empowerment (Department of Social Justice and Empowerment). 
2. The Sixth Report was presented to Lok Sabha and laid in Rajya Sabha on 
3rd March, 2020. The Department of Social Justice and Empowerment have 
furnished their replies indicating action taken on the recommendations contained 
in that Report on 3rd September, 2020. The Report was considered and adopted 
by the Standing Committee on Social Justice and Empowerment at their sitting 
held on 10th November, 2020. 
3. An analysis of the action taken by Government on the recommendations 
contained in the Sixth  Report of the Standing Committee on Social Justice and 
Empowerment (Seventeenth Lok Sabha) is given in Appendix. 
4. For facility of reference observations/recommendations/comments of the 
Committee have been printed in thick type in the body of the Report. 
  
     NEW DELHI;

CHAPTER - I 
1.1 This Report of the Standing Committee on Social Justice and Empowerment 
deals with the action taken by the Government on the observations/recommendations 
contained in the Twentieth Report of the Standing Committee on Social Justice and 
Empowerment (Seventeenth Lok Sabha) on Demands for Grants (2021-22) pertaining 
to the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment (Department of Social Justice and 
Empowerment). 
1.2 The Twentieth Report was presented to Lok Sabha and laid in Rajya Sabha on 
16th March, 2021. It con tained 10 observations/recommendations. Replies of 
Government in respect of all the observations/recommendations have been examined 
and are categorized as under: - 
(i) Observations/Recommendations which have been accepted by the Government: 
 
Paragraph Nos. 2.11, 3.17, 4.9, 4.10, 5.16 and 7.12 
 
                   (Total : 6 - Chapter-II) 
 
(ii) Observations/Recommendations which the Committee do not desire to 
pursue in view of the replies of the Government: 
Paragraph Nos. 2.10 and 6.14 
       (Total : 2 - Chapter-III) 
 
(iv) Observations/Recommendations in respect of which replies of the Government 
have not been accepted and which require reiteration: 
Paragraph No. 3.15 
(Total : 1 - Chapter-IV) 
 
(v) Observations/Recommendations in respect of which replies of the Government 
are of interim in nature:  
Paragraph No. 3.16 
(Total : 1 - Chapter- V) 

3 
 
 
1.3 The Committee desire that action taken notes o n the recommendations 
contained in Chapter-I and final action  taken note in respect of the 
recommendation contained in Chapter-V of this Report may be furnished to them 
at the earliest and in any case not later than three months of the presentation of 
this Report. 
 
1.4 The Committee will now deal with the replies received from the Government 
which need reiteration or merit comments. 
A. THE POST MATRIC SCHOLARSHIP SCHEME FOR SC STUDENTS (PMS-SC) 
Recommendation (Para No. 3.15) 
 
1.5 The Committee had recommended in their Twentieth Report as under:- 
“The 60 year old  Post  Matric  Scholarship Scheme  for Scheduled 
Caste students guarantees financial assistance to fulfill the aspirations of those 
Scheduled Caste Students whose parents’ income does not exceed ₹ 2.5 lakh  
annually. The Committee note that only  113.15 lakh students have benefitted during 
the last two years i.e., 2018-19  and 2019 -20 upto 31 st December, 2020 with an 
expenditure of ₹ 8639.47 crore under this Scheme. The Committee feel that the number 
of beneficiaries should be much more i.e., around  80 lakh per year  to realize the 
number of 4 crore students , projected to  be benefitted in the next  
5 years.  In the light of the decision that States have to give their share of 40 per cent of 
scholarships amount first and then the 60 per cent share of the Centre will be  released 
to   the   students, the   Committee were informed by the representatives of the Ministry 
that States liability has now been reduced and hence it is a welcome move.   
Nonetheless,   all   State   Governments   are   not   very efficient in giving their share on 
time, hence the Committee feel that an appropriate system may be developed so that 

4 
 
the students are not deprived of Scholarship in the absence or delay in providing share 
by the States. The Committee, therefore, recommend that adequate awareness may be  
created amongst the students so that maximum number of students are able to take the   
benefit   of   the   Scheme   particularly   in   view   of   the target fixed   for   next   five   
years.   The   C ommittee   also recommend that since the suggestion s made in the 
recently conducted Evaluation Study of the Scheme are practical and worthy of 
consideration, hence those may be examined and implemented.  The  Committee  also  
appreciate  the  concept  of   issuing   of   FreeShip   Card, after verification  of eligibility 
of the candidates under the Scheme,  as  this  will prove to be very beneficial for the 
students to take admission in the institution of their choice anywhere in the country   
without paying any fee. The Committee desire that the Department  should direct all the 
States/UTs to issue FreeShip Card to all the eligible students who have applied under 
the Scheme."

INTRODUCTION 
 
I, the Chair person, Standing Committee on  Social Justice and 
Empowerment (2019-20) having been authorized by the Committee to submit 
the Report on their behalf, do present this fifth Report on the action taken by 
the Government on the observations/recommendations contained in the Sixty-
third Report (Sixteenth Lok Sabha) of the Standing  Committee on Social 
Justice and Empowerment on "Assessment of the working of Tribal Sub -Plan 
(TSP)" of the Ministry of Tribal Affairs. 
2. The Sixty-third Report was presented to Lok Sabha and laid in Rajya 
Sabha on 03.01.2019. The Ministry of Tribal Affairs have furnished their replies 
indicating action taken on the recommendations contained in that Report on 
09.05.2019.  The Report was considered and adopted by the Standing 
Committee on Social Justice and Empowerment at their sitting held on  
10th December, 2019. 
3. An analysis of the action taken by Government on the recommendations 
contained in the Sixty-third Report (Sixteenth Lok Sabha) of the Standing 
Committee on Social Justice and Empowerment is given in Appendix. 
4. For facility of reference observations/recommendations/comments of 
the Committee have been printed in thick type in the body of the Report.

policy and planning, coordination, evaluation and review of the regulatory and 
development programmes for the benefit of the minority communities namely Jains, 
Parsis, Buddhists, Sikhs, Christians and Muslims.

the multi-facial, multi-cultural, multi-lingual and multi-religious character of the nation.

regulators. The Committee notes that these agencies have been striving to maintain safety oversight in 
alignment with the international standards prescribed by the International Civil Aviation Organisation 
(ICAO).

approximately 95 per cent of India’s trade by volume and 68 per cent by value. The Ministry 
of Ports, Shipping and Waterways exercises policy and regulatory oversight across this 
sector, encompassing port development, shipping regulation, shipbuilding promotion, ship 
repair and recycling, dredging, lighthouse administration, and inland water transport. The 
pace and quality of infrastructure modernisation, regulatory reform, and capacity creation 
within this sector have a direct bearing on the nation’s logistics costs, trade facilitation, and 
the objective of establishing India as a global maritime leader under the Maritime Amrit Kaal 
Vision 2047.

INTRODUCTION
 
I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Transport, Tourism and Culture,
 having been authorised by the Committee to present on its behalf, do hereby present this One Hundredth Report of the
 Committee on the Inland Vessels (Amendment) Bill, 2005*.
2.         In pursuance of rules relating to the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committees, the Hon’ble
 Chairman, Rajya Sabha referred** the Bill as introduced in the Rajya Sabha on the 8
th December, 2005 and pending
 therein, to the Committee on 13th December, 2005 for examination and report within three months.  On the request
 being made by the Chairman of the Committee, the Hon'ble Chairman, Rajya Sabha had granted extension of time upto
 30
th April, 2006 for the presentation of the Report of the Committee on the aforesaid Bill.
3.          The Committee took oral evidence of the Secretary and other officers of the Department of Shipping and
 Ministry of Law and Justice at its meeting held on the 12
th January, 2006.
4.         In order to get wider views on the subject, the Committee invited the views of individuals, organisations and
 institutions on the subject through advertisement in all major national dallies and vernacular newspapers all over the
 country.  The advertisement evoked tremendous public response and the Committee received memoranda on the subject
 for consideration of the Committee.  The Committee also heard the views of the representatives of the Goa Barge
 Owners Association, M/s. Sanghi Brothers (Indore) Ltd, Ganga Water Transport Company (Pvt.) Ltd., Eastern
 Navigation (Pvt.) Ltd., Vivada Inland Waterways Ltd. and Central Inland Water Transport Corporation Ltd. on the
 provisions of the Bill at its meeting held on the 1
st February 2006.
5.        The Committee took up clause-by-clause consideration of the Bill during its meeting held on the 17th March,
 2006.  The Committee also considered the draft Report on the subject and adopted the same with minor modifications
 on 17
th March, 2006 itself.
6.          The Committee wishes to express its thanks to the Secretary and other officers of the Department of Shipping
 and Ministry of Law and Justice for the assistance provided during deliberations on the provisions of the Bill.  The
 Committee also acknowledges the contribution of the representatives of various Associations/Stakeholders who
 submitted their valuable suggestions on the provisions of the Bill.

 Committee on the 17 th May, 2007 for examination and report within three months. On the request being made by the
 Chairman of the Committee, Hon’ble Chairman had granted extension of time till the first day of last week of the
 Budget Session (second part) of the Parliament for the presentation of the report of the Committee on the aforesaid Bill.

INTRODUCTION
I, the Chairman, Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Transport,
Tourism and Culture, having been authorized by the Committee to submit on its behalf, do hereby
present this One Hundred Forty Second Report on Functioning of Private Airports and related
issues.
2. The Government of India had decided to modernize and upgrade the existing domestic and
international airports at Mumbai and Delhi to world standards and to construct Greenfield airports
in Bangalore and Hyderabad through Public Private Partnership. The Greenfield airports in
Hyderabad and Bangalore have started functioning from the 23rd March and 24th May, 2008
respectively. The modernization of Delhi and Mumbai Airports are in different stages of
development.
3. There were a large number of reports/representations about the problems faced by the
passengers and associated agencies at Mumbai and Delhi Airports and also at Bengaluru and
Hyderabad after the new Greenfield airports were opened and the old ones were closed. The
Committee while discussing these issues felt it necessary to visit these airports for an on-the-
spot assessment of the problems and to see facilities available at these airports. Accordingly,
the Committee visited the new airports at Bengaluru, Hyderabad and Mumbai from the 14th to
20th September, 2008 on this issue. The Committee also visited the old airport at Begumpet, in
Hyderabad. The Committee had already visited the Delhi Airport on l0th January, 2008. The
Committee interacted with various stakeholders at these airports for finalizing its report.
4. Apart from passenger amenities, the Committee has also dealt with various issues/points
relating to the policy of privatization of airports, procedures adopted for this and other related
matters.
5. The Committee wishes to express its thanks to the representatives of the Ministry of Civil
Aviation, Airports Authority of India, managements of Bangalore International Airport Ltd. (BIAL),
Hyderabad International Airport Ltd. (HIAL), Mumbai International Airport Ltd. (MIAL) and Delhi
International Airport Ltd. (DIAL) for placing before the Committee the material and information

Tourism and Culture, having been authorised by the Committee, do hereby present on its behalf
this One Hundred Forty-ninth Report on ‘Development of Tourism Infrastructure and Amenities for
the Commonwealth Games 2010’,

is expected to attract one lakh foreign tourists to Delhi during this period. As the Commonwealth
Games is expected to have large scale impact on India's tourism Sector, the Committee decided
to take stock of the preparedness and efforts of the Government and various stakeholders for
providing the tourists all the facilities including infrastructure development, transport infrastructure
and connectivity, conservation and preservation of monument, hotel accommodation and human
resource development etc. for making the event successful.

Tourism and Culture, having been authorized by the Committee to present on its behalf, do hereby
present this One Hundred and Fiftieth Report of the Committee on the National Commission for
Heritage Sites Bill, 2009*.

INTRODUCTION
I, the Chairman, Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Transport,
Tourism and Culture, having been authorised by the Committee, do hereby present on its behalf
this One Hundred Sixty Seventh Report on ‘Functioning of National Museum’.
2. The Committee had decided to examine the functioning of National Museum in view of
certain feedback received about its facilities and upkeep. The Committee visited National Museum
on 14
th September, 2010.
5. The Committee held discussions with the Ministry of Culture and CPWD on
30th September, 2010. The Committee expresses its gratitude to the officers of the Ministry of
Culture and National Museum for their cooperation in furnishing the required feedback and
information in connection with the examination of the subject.
4. The Committee considered and adopted the Report at its meeting held on the 25
th January, 2011.
SITARAM YECHURY
NEW D ELHI; Chairman,
January 25, 2011 Department-related Parliamentary Standing
Magha 5, 1932  (Saka) Committee on Transport, Tourism and Culture.

1
REPORT
1. The National Museum which was formally inaugurated in August, 1949 in Delhi has in its
possession over 2 lakhs works of exquisite art, both Indian and foreign origin, covering more than
5000 years of cultural heritage. The Museum houses collections of Pre-historic Archaeology,
Archaeology, Anthropology, Jewellery, Paintings, Decorative Arts, Manuscript, Central Asian
Antiquities, Numismatics, Arms and Armour pre-Columbian and Western Art epigraphy, etc. The
National Museum initially housed at the Rashtrapati Bhavan, was shifted to its present building at
Janpath in the year 1960. It is now within the administrative control and fully financed by the
Ministry of Culture, Government of India.
2. National Museum was set up with the following vision:-
(i) To Collect antiquities and art objects of historical, cultural and artistic significance for
their protection, preservation and research;
(ii) To disseminate knowledge about significance of the objects, their history, culture and
artistic excellence;
(iii) To serve as a cultural center for enjoyment and interaction of people in and around

INTRODUCTION
I, the Chairman, Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Transport,
Tourism and Culture, having been authorised by the Committee to present on its behalf, do hereby
present this One Hundred and Sixty Eighth Report on “Directorate General of Civil Aviation
(DGCA)–Issues and Challenges”.
2. The Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Transport, Tourism and
Culture in its meeting held on the 15
th September, 2009 decided to have an in-depth study on the
functioning of Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA). The subject selected was notified in
Parliamentary Bulletin Part II dated the 1
st October, 2009.
3. Apart from a detailed background note obtained from the Ministry of Civil Aviation, the
Committee heard the views of the Secretary, Ministry of Civil Aviation, Director General of Civil
Aviation, CMD, Air India Limited and Chairman, Airports Authority of India in its meetings held on
the 8
th January, 29 th June and 8 th October, 2010. In order to get wider views on the subject, the
Committee invited the views of individuals, organisations and institutions on the subject through
advertisement in all major national dailies and vernacular newspapers all over the country.
4. The Committee wishes to express its thanks to the Secretary and other officers of the
Ministry of Civil Aviation for providing necessary inputs and clarifications during deliberations on
the subject. The Committee also acknowledges the contribution of the individuals/Associations who
submitted their valuable suggestions on the subject.
5. The Committee considered and adopted the Report at its meeting held on the 13
th April, 2011.

INTRODUCTION
I, the Chairman, Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Transport, Tourism
and Culture, having been authorised by the Committee, do hereby present on its behalf this One
Hundred Seventy Second Report on ‘Development of Tourism in the North-East Region’.
2. India’s North-East has the potential to become an attractive tourist destination because of its
unique geographical distribution and peculiar flora and fauna. However, this tourism potential is not
properly developed and exploited. The Committee, in continuation to its special focus on promotion
of Tourism in India, took up the State of Jammu and Kashmir in the first phase with its l40
th Report
and now the North-Eastern Region as a second step. Accordingly, the Committee undertook a study
visit to Guwahati, Aizawl, Shillong and Agartala from 9
th to 15 th February, 2011. Regarding other States
of the region, the Committee interacted with the State Government and other agencies connected with
the tourism sector at Delhi.
3. The Committee emphasized on the tourism infrastructure, trained man-power, development and
maintenances of national highways in the Region; increasing air connectivity and expansion/modernization
of airports and protection and preservation of ancient monuments for the enhancement of tourist flow
to the Region. The Committee was apprised of the difficulties that came in the way of promotion of
tourism in the Region such as restriction of entry of tourist, poor infrastructure, lack of transport
facility, poor security and road-rail-air network etc. The Committee, therefore, decided to present a
report focusing mainly on these aspects.

INTRODUCTION
I, the Chairman, Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Transport,
Tourism and Culture, having authorized by the Committee to present on its behalf, do hereby
present this One Hundred Eighty Ninth Report on “Development of National Waterways—Potential
and Challenges”.
2. Even though India is endowed with navigable waterways comprising rivers, canals, back
waters etc., as a means of transport it is operational only in restricted stretches of Ganga-
Bhagirathi-Hooghly Rivers, the Brahmaputra river, the Barak river, rivers in Goa, the back waters
in Kerala, inland waters in Mumbai and the deltaic regions of the Godavari-Krishna rivers. As such
for taking an in-depth view on the potential and the ailments in the sector, the Department-related
Parliamentary Standing Committee on Transport, Tourism and Culture decided to take up the
examination of the Inland Water Transport System in the country.
3. On 18
th October, 2012, the Committee heard the Secretary, Ministry of Shipping and
Chairman, Inland Waterways Authority of India to get an overview of the subject. The Committee
also interacted with the stakeholders and beneficiaries like NTPC, ONGC, FICCI, FACT etc., for
taking their views on the subject.
4. The Committee wishes to express its thanks to the Secretary and other officers of the
Ministry of Shipping and Inland Waterways Authority of India

INTRODUCTION
I, the Chairman, Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Transport,
Tourism and Culture, do hereby present on its behalf this Two Hundredth Report  on ‘Development
of Tourism, National Highways and Water Transport in Kerala and Cochin Shipyard Limited’.
2. Kerala, with its uniqueness has become one of the major popular tourist destinations of the
world. The tourism industry’s contribution to the state’s economy is also commendable. However,
a need was evident to channalise Kerala’s tourism potential into a customized revenue harnessing
source without disturbing natural environment and by enhancing the cultural integrity of local
people. The Committee, in continuation to its special focus on promotion of Tourism in various
regions of India, took up the study visit to a few of tourist destinations in Kerala i.e., Kochi,
Munnar and Thekkady, between 24
th to 31 st May, 2013. The Committee made similar studies
previously on North-East region and Jammu and Kashmir.
3. The Committee examined various issues such as Cruise, Wellness, Medical, Wildlife, Tea
and Eco tourism of Kerala, Spice route and Muziris heritage projects, Rationalization of Inter-State
tourist permits, Heavy taxation, Comprehensive waste management, National Highways issues, River
tourism and linking of ports on NW3, IWT connectivity to ICTT. The Committee noted the
difficulties in achieving these objectives viz., Non-availability of Visa-on arrival, Promoting of
tourist destinations of Kerala nationally and internationally, Limited air connectivity, Maintenance and
construction of national highways, Rail-road-waterway linkages, Maintenance dredging, etc.
4. The Committee also took up the study of Cochin Shipyard Limited and examined the
challenges it is facing in Shipbuilding and Ship repair sectors.

I, the Chairman, Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Transport,
Tourism and Culture, having been authorised by the Committee to present on its behalf, do hereby
present this Two Hundred and Eelventh Report on “Upkeep of various Monuments in Delhi,
National Museum and other important issues pertaining to the Ministry of Culture”.
2. The Committee in the first chapter of this Report has dealt with upkeep of various
important monuments in Delhi. Most of the issues raised here were under examination of the
Committee for a long time and recently the Committee heard the views of the Ministry of Tourism,
Ministry of Culture, Aga Khan Trust for Culture, Archaeological Survey of India and INTACH on
27
th January, 2014 on the subject. Similarly, the portion pertaining to the National Museum is also
based on the replies received from the Ministry of Culture on the 167 th and the 179 th Reports of
the Committee. Given the crucial importance of the subject, the Committee has made further
observations/recommendations in this Report for follow up action.
3. The Committee has also dealt with several outstanding issues on which recommendations
were given in various Reports earlier but, those have not been implemented fully. The Committee
understands that if implemented, it will go a long way in protecting the cultural heritage of the
country and the interface of culture with tourism will certainly be better.

written and oral replies/submissions on different occasions. The Committee is also thankful to Aga

INTRODUCTION
I, the Chairman, Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Transport,
Tourism and Culture, having been authorized by the Committee, do hereby present on its behalf
this Two Hundred Thirty Sixth Report on “Infrastructure Lending in Road Sector”.
2. The Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Transport, Tourism and
Culture decided to take up the Infrastructure Lending in Road Sector for examination and Report,
as it is felt that roads projects are getting delayed due to various reasons and the Committee tries
to find out the reasons for slow growth of this sector.
3. The Committee heard the views of the Central Engineering Services Group ‘A ’ Officers’
Association, National Highways Builders Federation on the issue on 16th April, 2015.  The
Committee, thereafter, heard the views of the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways and
National Highways Authority of India on 1st October, 2015.  The Committee also heard the views
of the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways, National Highways Authority of India,  Ministry
of Finance, Reserve Bank of India, Punjab National Bank and Oriental Bank of Commerce on the
18th February, 2016.
4. The Committee visited Kolkata, Mumbai and Kodaikanal from 31st May to 7th June, 2015
to study the subject i.e. Infrastructure Lending in Road Sector.  The Committee heard the views
of Reserve Bank of India, Union Bank of India, Central Bank of India, State Bank of India, Bank
of Baroda, Bank of India, I.D.B.I., IIFCIL, IFCI, LIC, PERDA, NHAI, Highways Constructors;
Association, Government of Maharashtra at Mumbai on 3rd June, 2015. The Committee also visited
Mumbai and Kochi from 12th 18th October, 2015 and in Kochi the Committee heard the views of
NHAI, Ministry of Road Transport and Highways, State Government of Kerala, State Bank of
Travancore, Syndicate Bank on the subject on 17th October, 2015. The Committee also visited
Goa, Hyderabad and Bengaluru from 31st January to 7th Februa

of Civil Aviation Security . The functions pertaining to railway safety are entrusted to a 
Commission viz. Commission of Railway Safety .

INTRODUCTION 
 
 I, the Chairman of the Department -related Parliamentary Standing Committee 
on Transport, Tourism and Culture, having been authorised by the Committee to 
present on its behalf, do hereby present this Two Hundred Thirty Ninth  Report of the 
Committee on the  Motor Vehicles (Amendment) Bill, 2016*. 
2.         The Bill was introduced in the Lok Sabha on the 9th August, 2016.  In pursuance 
of rules relating to the Department -related Parliamentary Standing Committees, the 
Hon‟ble Chairman, Rajya Sabha, referred** the Bill to the Committee on the 17 th 
August, 2016 for examination and report within two months. On the request being 
made by the Chairman of the Committee, Hon‟ble Chairman had granted extension of 
time for a period of two months i.e. upto 16th December, 2016.  But the deliberations 
could not be concluded within the stipulated period and the Committee again requested 
extension.  The Hon‟ble Chairman, Rajya Sabha acceded to the request for the 
presentation of the Report to both the Houses of the Parliament upto 16 th February, 
2017. 
3.          The Committee took oral evidence of the Secretary and other officers of the 
Ministry of Road Transport and Highways and Ministry of Law and Justice at its 
meeting held on the 29 th September and 14 th October, 2016.  The Committee heard the 
views of Secretaries, Ministries  of Road Transport and Transport Commissioner s  of 
various States and Union Territories  on 25 th October, 2016 and 4 th November, 2016. 
The Committee also heard the views of the representatives of various stakeholders and 
individuals at its meeting held on the 4th November, 2016. 
4. The Committee considered the draft Report on the Bill in its meetings held on 
9th December and 27th December, 2016 and adopted the same on  24th January, 2017. 
5.          The Committee wishes to express its thanks to the Secretary and other officers 
of the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways and Ministry of Law and Justice for 
the assistance and inputs provided during delibe rations on the provisions of the Bill.

and Culture, having been authorised by the Committee to present on its behalf, do hereby present this

request being made by the Chairman of the Committee, Hon'ble Chairman had granted extension of time
for a period of three months, i.e., upto 12th July, 2017.

Ministry of Law and Justice in its meeting held on the 25th April, 2017 on various provision of the Bill.

representatives of trade associations, Ship Owners' Associations, Shipping Lines Association, Private
Ports Associations etc. on the 3rd May, 2017. The Committee also undertook a study visit to Ahmedabad,
Mumbai and Kochi from 4th to 10th June, 2017 and heard the views of all the Major Port Trusts, Port

stakeholders and individuals.

REPORT 
The Department of Tourism is the nodal agency for the formulation of national policies 
and programmes on tourism and for the coordination of activities of various Central 
Government agencies, State Governments and Private sector for the development of tourism 
in the country. The main activities of the Department are: 
(i) Policy forn1ulation and planning. 
(ii) Co-ordination . 
(iii) Regulation. 
(iv) Infrastructural and Product development. 
(v) Human Resource Development. 
(vi) Publicity, Marketing and Facilitation. 
(vii) Research, Analysis, Monitoring & Evaluation. 
(viii) International Cooperation & External Assistance. 
(ix) Legislation and Parliament Work. 
(x) Management of Public Sector Undertakings & autonomous bodies. 
2. The Department of Tourism is assisted by the Director General of Tourism, an ex­
officio Additional Secretary to Government of India. The Department has under its 
administrative control the following public sector undertakings/autonomous bodies: 
(i) India Tourism Development Corporation Ltd.; 
(ii) National Council for Hotel Management ; 
(iii) Indian Institute of Tourism & Travel Management; 
(iv) Institutes of Hotel Management, Catering Technology and Applied Nutrition al 
different locations in the country; 
(v) Food Craft InstiTUtes at different locations; 
(vi) Indian InstiTUte of Skiing & Mountaineering; and 
(vii) National Institute of Water Sports. 
3. The office of the Director General has a field formation of 18 offices abroad and 21 
offices within the country. Overseas offices are primarily responsible for tourism promotion 
and marketing in their respective nreos, while the field offices in India are responsible for 
providing information services to tourists and to monitor the process ?f field projects

ii 
 
 
INTRODUCTION 
 
 I, the Chairman, Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Transport, 
Tourism and Culture, having been authorized by the Committee to present on its behalf, do 
hereby present this Three Hundred Forty-Eighth Report on 'Heritage Theft – The Illegal 
Trade in Indian Antiquities and the Challenges of Retrieving and Safeguarding Our Tangible 
Cultural Heritage'.  
2. The Committee heard the views of the representatives of Indian National Trust for Art 
and Cultural Heritage (INTACH) , on the subject on 15th November, 2022. The Committee 
also heard the views of the Senior Officers of Ministry of Culture and Archaeological Survey 
of India, on the subject on 25th November, 2022. The Committee in its third meeting on the 
subject, held on 22nd December, 2022, heard the views of the Senior Officers of Directorate 
of Enforcement (ED); Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs  (CBIC); and Directorate 
of Revenue Intelligence (DRI) . The Committee also heard the representatives of Department 
of Legal Affairs, Ministry of Home Affairs and Ministry of External Affairs , on the subject 
on 5th January, 2023.  
3.  The Committee wishes to express its thanks to the officers of Ministry of Culture; 
Archaeological Survey of India; Ministry of Home Affairs;  Ministry of External Affairs; 
Department of Legal Affairs; Directorate of Enforcement; Central Board of Indirect Taxes & 
Customs; Directorate of Revenue Intelligence; and Indian National Trust for Art and Cultural 
Heritage for placing before the Committee , the material and information desired in 
connection with the subject and for clarifying the points raised by the Members. 
4. The Committee considered and adopted the Report in its meeting held on the  8th May, 
2023.

Tourism and Culture, having been authorized by the Committee to present on its behalf, do 
hereby present this Three Hundred Fifty Seventh Rep ort on ‘Development of Niche Tourism 
(including Spiritual Tourism), Theme-based Tourist Circuits and Potential Tourist Spots’.

the subject, on 26 th  June, 2023. The Committee also heard the views of the representatives of 
the Federation of Hotel and Restaurant Associations  of India (FHRAI); Indian Association of 
Tour Operators (IATO); Indian Tourist Transporters Association (ITTA); and Adventure 
Tour Operators Association of India (ATOAI), in its  meeting on the subject, held on 18 th  
July, 2023. Further, the Committee heard the views of the representatives of the Ministry of

REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE
I, the chairman of the Committee on Transport and Tourism, having been authorised by the Committee, present this
 thirty Sixth Report of the Committee relating to the Major Port Trusts (Amendment) Bill, 1998. The Bill seeks to
 amend section 42 (sub section 1 & 3 ) and section 88 (sub section 2) of the Major Port Trusts Act, 1963, which
 provides privatisation and to enable implementation of the joint venture scheme.
2. In pursuance of the rules relating to the Department-Related Parliamentary Standing Committee, the Hon’ble
 Chairman, Rajya Sabha referred * the Bill, as introduced in the Rajya Sabha on the 2nd December, 1998and pending
 therein to the Committee for examination and report thereon.
3. The Committee discussed the provisions of the Bill at its meeting held on 19
th January 1999.
4. The Committee heard the views of the Secretary Ministry of Surface Transport on the subject.
5. The Committee also heard the views of the Board of Trustees and workers unions of some of the Major Ports.
6. The Committee also deliberated upon the petition which was forwarded by the Committee on Petitions, Rajya Sabha,
 received by them from the All India Port and Dock workers Federation and countersigned by Smt. Kamla Sinha and
 Shri Jibon Roy, Member of Parliament, Rajya Sabha, in connection with the said Bill.
7. The Committee decided that the evidence tendered by the Secretary Ministry of Surface Transport before the
 Committee should be laid on the table of both the Houses of Parliament.
8. The Committee while considering the Bill took note of the following documents furnished by the Ministry of Surface
 Transport.
(i) Background note on the Bill.
(ii) Guidelines to be followed by Major Port Trusts for Private
Sector Participation in the Major Ports.
(iii) Guidelines for Private Sector Participation in Ports through
Joint ventures and Foreign Collaborations.
9. The Committee, at its meeting held on 26
th February, 1999, discussed the provisions of the Bill and took
 up clause by clause consideration thereof.
10. The Committee was informed of the Objects and Reasons for amendment of the Act. The Committee was also
 explained that Ninety percent of India’s sea trade is conducted through eleven Major Ports in the country which are
 administered by the respective Board of Trustees constituted under Major Port Trusts Act 1963. The Committee was
 apprised that the Sea traffic at the ports has been increasing steadily over the past years.
It was explained to the Committee that on a conservative estimate of cumulative growth of 9% per annum in term of
 traffic, our ports must be capable of handling a traffic of approximately 850 MT by 2012. This would require 300 to
 400 additional berths to handle the cargo of different kinds. The creation of additional port capacity of this magnitude at
 the current costs would require an investment of over rupees 40,000 crores. Projections undertaken by the Ministry of
 Surface Transport indicate that not more than rupees 12,000 crores would be available from plan funds and the internal
 resources of the ports for investment in port development and the balance would have to come from the private sector
 or from the capital market.
The Central Government had announced guidelines for private sector participation in the Major Ports in October,1996.

 and the owners of foreign ports, minor ports or any company. These measures; apart from enhancing confidence of

(i) Attract new technology.
(ii) Introduce better managerial practices.
(iii) Expedite implementation of schemes and;
(iv) Foster strategic alliance with minor ports for creation of optimal port infrastructure.
To achieve the aforesaid purpose, it is proposed to amend the Major Port Trust Act, 1963.
