REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE
I, the chairman of the Committee on Transport and Tourism, having been authorised by the Committee, present this
 thirty Sixth Report of the Committee relating to the Major Port Trusts (Amendment) Bill, 1998. The Bill seeks to
 amend section 42 (sub section 1 & 3 ) and section 88 (sub section 2) of the Major Port Trusts Act, 1963, which
 provides privatisation and to enable implementation of the joint venture scheme.
2. In pursuance of the rules relating to the Department-Related Parliamentary Standing Committee, the Hon’ble
 Chairman, Rajya Sabha referred * the Bill, as introduced in the Rajya Sabha on the 2nd December, 1998and pending
 therein to the Committee for examination and report thereon.
3. The Committee discussed the provisions of the Bill at its meeting held on 19
th January 1999.
4. The Committee heard the views of the Secretary Ministry of Surface Transport on the subject.
5. The Committee also heard the views of the Board of Trustees and workers unions of some of the Major Ports.
6. The Committee also deliberated upon the petition which was forwarded by the Committee on Petitions, Rajya Sabha,
 received by them from the All India Port and Dock workers Federation and countersigned by Smt. Kamla Sinha and
 Shri Jibon Roy, Member of Parliament, Rajya Sabha, in connection with the said Bill.
7. The Committee decided that the evidence tendered by the Secretary Ministry of Surface Transport before the
 Committee should be laid on the table of both the Houses of Parliament.
8. The Committee while considering the Bill took note of the following documents furnished by the Ministry of Surface
 Transport.
(i) Background note on the Bill.
(ii) Guidelines to be followed by Major Port Trusts for Private
Sector Participation in the Major Ports.
(iii) Guidelines for Private Sector Participation in Ports through
Joint ventures and Foreign Collaborations.
9. The Committee, at its meeting held on 26
th February, 1999, discussed the provisions of the Bill and took
 up clause by clause consideration thereof.
10. The Committee was informed of the Objects and Reasons for amendment of the Act. The Committee was also
 explained that Ninety percent of India’s sea trade is conducted through eleven Major Ports in the country which are
 administered by the respective Board of Trustees constituted under Major Port Trusts Act 1963. The Committee was
 apprised that the Sea traffic at the ports has been increasing steadily over the past years.
It was explained to the Committee that on a conservative estimate of cumulative growth of 9% per annum in term of
 traffic, our ports must be capable of handling a traffic of approximately 850 MT by 2012. This would require 300 to
 400 additional berths to handle the cargo of different kinds. The creation of additional port capacity of this magnitude at
 the current costs would require an investment of over rupees 40,000 crores. Projections undertaken by the Ministry of
 Surface Transport indicate that not more than rupees 12,000 crores would be available from plan funds and the internal
 resources of the ports for investment in port development and the balance would have to come from the private sector
 or from the capital market.
The Central Government had announced guidelines for private sector participation in the Major Ports in October,1996.

REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE

 and the owners of foreign ports, minor ports or any company. These measures; apart from enhancing confidence of
 private sector in funding ports, are aimed at facilitating the Major Ports to:-
(i) Attract new technology.
(ii) Introduce better managerial practices.
(iii) Expedite implementation of schemes and;
(iv) Foster strategic alliance with minor ports for creation of optimal port infrastructure.
To achieve the aforesaid purpose, it is proposed to amend the Major Port Trust Act, 1963.
11. The Ministry of Surface Transport also in their background note submitted to the Committee explained the need for
 introduction of the Bill and the provision to be made in the Bill as under: -
(a) It is proposed to insert clause (f) in sub-section 1 of section 42 of the Act to bring the supporting infrastructure; such

I N T R O D U C T I O N
 
            I, the Chairman, Standing Committee on Transport and Tourism, having been authorised by the Committee to present on their behalf, present this Thirty-Seventh Report on the
 Demands for Grants 1999-2000 of the Ministry of Tourism.           
2. The Committee at its meeting held on 23rd  March,1999, considered the Demands for Grants 1999-2000 of the Ministry of Tourism  and heard the Secretary, the Ministry of 
 Tourism on the subject. 
3.The Committee expresses its thanks to the officers of the Ministry for placing before the Committee, the material and information desired in connection with the examination of the
 Demands for Grants of the Ministry and for giving evidence before the Committee. 
4.The Committee considered and adopted the Report at its meeting held on the 7
th April, 1999.
 
 
New Delhi                                                                                         PROF. VIJAY KUMAR MALHOTRA
7
TH April,1999                                                                                                        Chairman
Chaitra 17,1921(Saka)                                                                   Committee on Transport & Tourism 
  
 
REPORT
 
 
Demand No. 82 pertains to the Ministry of Tourism.  The Ministry of Tourism in their written note has informed that tourism is a major social phenomenon of the modern society with
 enormous economic consequences.  Its importance as an instrument for economic development and employment generation particularly in remote and backward areas has been now
 well recognised the world over. 
The provisions in this demand mainly include allocations for the Secretariat of the Ministry of Tourism, the expenditure on the headquarter establishment of the Directorate General of
 Tourism and the regional and field offices under it, expenditure on production and publicity material for the promotional programmes, both domestic and overseas; provisions for
 creation of infrastructural facilities like Tourist Bungalows, Yatri Niwas, Wayside Amenities etc. and Grants in Aid to the various Tourism Training Institutes of the Ministry of
 Tourism. The Director General of Tourism functions as the nodal agency for the formulation of national policies and programmes and the coordination of activities of various Central
 Government agencies, State Governments and the Private Sector for the development and growth of Tourism in the country. 
Tourism is the world’s largest export industry.  According to the World Tourism Organisation, about 612.8 million tourists travel internationally in 1997 and spent about US$ 444
 billion.  It is estimated that tourism accounts for about 8% of the total world exports and more than 30% of international trade in services.  In 1997-98 travel and tourism was expected
 to provide direct and indirect employment for 212 million people and accounted for 10.7% of the global work force. 
The international tourist traffic to India during 1951 was just 16,829.  Over a period of 46 years, the arrivals increased to 2.37 million in 1997 and registered a compounded annual rate
 of growth of about 3.8%.  The foreign exchange earnings from tourism during 1997-98 was estimated to be about Rs.11,264 crores (US $ 3173 million).  The rate of growth in foreign
 exchange earning from tourism is exceptionally high.  The foreign exchange earnings for 1998-99 is projected to be Rs.12215.19 crores. During the Eighth Five Year Plan period, the
 foreign tourist arrivals including the nationals of Pakistan and Bangladesh recorded an annual growth of 5.6%.  The growth rate in arrivals, exclusive of nationals of Pakistan and
 Bangladesh, was 8.1%.  During the year 1997-98,  tourist arrivals were 23,70,985 inclusive of the nationals of Pakistan and Bangladesh as compared to 23,34,438 during 1996-97.  
The most significant feature of the tourism industry is its capacity to generate large scale employment opportunities particularly in remote and backward areas as it is a labour intensive
 industry.  It offers enormous potential for economically utilising the natural attractions like landscapes, mountains, beaches, rivers, etc. which would otherwise remain either idle or
 underutilised.  It also applies to a multitude of man-made attractions like monuments, palaces, forts and unique rural and city environments. 
The Ministry of Tourism has under its administrative control the following public sector undertakings/autonomous bodies:- 
India Tourism Development Corporation Limited
National Council for Hotel Management and Catering Technology
Indian Institute of Tourism & Travel Management
Institutes of Hotel Management, Catering Technology and Applied Nutrition at different locations in the country
Food Craft Institutes at different locations
Indian Institute of Skiing & Mountaineering

REPORT
 
The Ministry of Civil Aviation formulates national policies and programmes for the development and regulation of Civil
 Aviation and is responsible for devising and implementing schemes for orderly growth and expansion of civil air
 transport.  Its functions also extend to overseeing the provisions of airport facilities, air traffic services and carriage of
 passengers and goods by air.  The Ministry is also administratively responsible for the Commission of Railway Safety,
 a statutory body set up under the Indian Railways Act.
2. The Civil Aviation sector is monitored and regulated by two separate organisations under the Department of Civil
 Aviation i.e. Directorate General of Civil Aviation and Bureau of Civil Aviation Security.
3. The following public sector undertakings/companies/autonomous bodies also function under the administrative
 control of the Ministry of Civil Aviation:
(a) Air India Limited and its wholly owned subsidiaries viz., Hotel Corporation of India Ltd. and Air India Charters Ltd.
(b) Indian Airlines Limited and its wholly owned subsidiary viz. Airlines Allied Services Ltd.
(C)  Airports Authority of India.
(D)  Pawan Hans Helicopters Limited.
4.   Under Demand No.7 a budget allocation of Rs. 218.77 crores has been provided for the Ministry of Civil Aviation
 for the year 1999-2000 (Rs. 55 crores on plan side and Rs. 163.77 crores on non-plan side.)
5.  Provision in this demand mainly include allocations for the Secretariat of the Ministry, the establishment 
 expenditure and procurement of equipment and accessories for DGCA, Bureau of Civil Aviation Security, release of
 budgetary support to Airport Authority of India for improvement of operational facilities in the North Eastern region
 and other crucial areas and upgradation of Amritsar Airport, for making payment of share of FTT to AAI, subsidy for
 operation of Haj Charters, Grant-in-aid to Indira Gandhi Rashtriya Uran Acadamy and token amount of Rs. 1 lakh for
 each Indian Airlines and Air India. The annual plan of Hotel Corporation of  India is financed by Air India Ltd. and that
 of  IGRUA equally by Air India and Indian Airlines.

INTRODUCTION 
 
 I, the Chairman, Department -related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Transport, 
Tourism and Culture, having been authorized by the Committee to present on its behalf, do hereby 
present this Three Hundred Eightieth Report on ‘Overall Review of Safety in the Civil Aviation 
Sector’. 
2. The Committee heard the views of the Secretary, Ministry of Civil Aviation, during its 
meeting held on 9th July, 2025. It also took evidence from the representatives of the Directorate 
General of Civil Aviation (DGCA), Airpor ts Authority of India (AAI), Bureau of Civil Aviation 
Security (BCAS), Aircraft Accident Investigation Bureau (AAIB), airline CEOs, airport directors and 
regulators. The Committee notes that these agencies have been striving to maintain safety oversight in 
alignment with the international standards prescribed by the International Civil Aviation Organisation 
(ICAO). 
3. The Committee places on record its appreciation to the representatives of the Ministry of 
Civil Aviation and associated aviation bodies for furnishing the requisite information and materials on 
the subject and for providing clarifications on the issues raised by the Members during the 
deliberations. 
4. The Committee considered and adopted the Report in its meeting held on the 19th August, 
2025.

 Committee, to present on its behalf this Three Hundred  and  Eighty-Sixth 
 Report on the subject “Holistic Development  of India’s Tourism Sector

2. The Committee selected this subject in view of the growing strategic importance of 
tourism as a pillar of economic growth, employment generation, cultural preservation, 
and India’s global engagement. Tourism is uniquely positioned as a sector that 
integrates infrastructure, services, heritage, livelihoods, and soft power. The 
Committee notes that while physical infrastructure and destination promotion have 
received sustained policy attention in recent years, the human dimension of tourism 
has not evolved at a commensurate pace. 
 
3. The Committee is of the considered view that the future trajectory of India’s tourism 
sector will be determined not merely by the creation of assets, but by the quality, 
integrity, and professionalism of the human interfaces through which tourists 
experience the country. Guides, hospitality professionals, destination managers, 
cultural interpreters, and facilitators collectively shape visitor perception. Deficiencies 
in training, ethical conduct, and career structures in these roles directly erode trust and 
suppress tourism’s economic potential.

INTRODUCTION 
1. I, the Chairman, Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Transport, 
Tourism and Culture, having been authorised by the Committee, present this Report on the 
Demands for Grants (2026-27) of the Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways (Demand 
No. 78). 
2. The Committee examined the Demands for Grants in the context of the strategic centrality 
of the maritime sector to India’s economic architecture, trade competitiveness, and logistical 
efficiency. India possesses a coastline of 11,098 km, 12 Major Ports, approximately 217 
other-than-major ports, and 111 declared National Waterways. The maritime sector transports 
approximately 95 per cent of India’s trade by volume and 68 per cent by value. The Ministry 
of Ports, Shipping and Waterways exercises policy and regulatory oversight across this 
sector, encompassing port development, shipping regulation, shipbuilding promotion, ship 
repair and recycling, dredging, lighthouse administration, and inland water transport. The 
pace and quality of infrastructure modernisation, regulatory reform, and capacity creation 
within this sector have a direct bearing on the nation’s logistics costs, trade facilitation, and 
the objective of establishing India as a global maritime leader under the Maritime Amrit Kaal 
Vision 2047. 
3. The Committee’s scrutiny was directed not merely at the adequacy of financial allocations 
but at the structural coherence between budgetary intent and ground-level outcomes. 
Particular attention was devoted to: the absorptive capacity of the Ministry for an 
unprecedented 78 per cent increase in net GBS; the operationalisation of three new schemes

INTRODUCTION 
 
 I, the Chairman, Department -related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Transport, 
Tourism and Culture, having been author ised by the Committee, have the honour to present on 
its behalf this Report on the Demands for Grants (2026 -27) of the Ministry of Road Transport 
and Highways (Demand No.86). The Report has been prepared following a structured scrutiny 
of the Ministry's bu dgetary proposals for the financial year 2026 -27, in accordance with the 
mandate vested in the Committee under Rule 270 and related provisions of the Rules of 
Procedure and Conduct of Business in the Council of States. 
 
2. The Committee has examined the Demands for Grants of the Ministry in view of the 
central and catalytic role that Road Transport and Highway Infrastructure occupies in India's 
economic architecture. With a National Highway network exceeding 1,46,000 km and an 
annual capital outlay of Rs.  2,94,167.45 crore proposed for 2026 -27, the Ministry of Road 
Transport and Highways administers one of the largest infrastructure programmes in the world. 
The quality, pace and efficiency of its expenditure has a direct bearing on logistics costs, 
industrial competitiveness, agricultural market access, regional integration and the living 
standards of communities traversed by the national highway network. 
 
3. The Committee is of the considered view that the future trajectory of India's highway 
programme will be determined not merely by the quantum of capital mobilised but by the 
rigour with which it is planned, targeted and executed. The transition from a phase of rapid 
network expansion to one that prioritises quality assurance, long -term asset preserva tion, 
logistical efficiency and road safety represents a maturing of infrastructure policy. The 
Committee's scrutiny has accordingly been directed not only at the adequacy of financial 
allocations, but at the alignment between budgetary intent and ground -level outcomes with 
particular attention to recurring patterns of under -utilization in maintenance and research, the 
pace of completion of ongoing projects and the equity of regional distribution of infrastructure 
investment.

REPORT
 
The Committee on Transport and Tourism, at its meeting held on Tuesday, the 11th August 1998, decided to undertake
 the examination of the problems faced by both the foreign & domestic passengers/tourists at the airports while
 negotiating various mandatory clearances like Customs/Immigration/Visa/Foreign exchange etc.  Besides this, the
 Committee felt that the travelling public also encounters problems in the use of several facilities like
 Transport/Luggage Trolleys, toilets, drinking water, restaurants, medical aid, enquiry counter for assistance etc.  The
 Committee is of the view that the general opinion about the functioning of the airports amongst the travelling public is
 very poor.  The services provided at the airport are not upto the mark as compared to international standards and as
 such these need adequate improvements.
2.            Keeping in view the public importance of the subject, the Committee on Transport and Tourism issued
 advertisements in the leading newspapers all over the country as well as on Doordarshan/All India Radio seeking
 personal experience, suggestions of the public and views of the leading tour and travel operators regarding the
 difficulties/ harassment faced by the foreign/domestic passengers/tourists in availing the various facilities like visa,
 customs, immigration, foreign exchange, transport, shopping, security, general amenities etc. presently made available
 at the airports in the country.
3.         The advertisement issued in the newspapers/Doordarshan/All India Radio evoked encouraging response from the
 general public as well as from the leading Tour & Travel operators.  A total number of 132 memoranda were received
 containing the personal experiences of the travelling public and suggestions for improvements in the running of the
 airports.
4.         The Committee held discussions with the Ministry of Civil Aviation and Airports Authority of India.  The
 Committee also heard the views of the Ministries of Home Affairs, Finance (Department of Revenue) and External
 Affairs, which are directly related to the management of many mandatory clearances, which a tourist has to obtain at
 the international airports in the country.
5.         The Committee also heard the views of leading Tour & Travel operators/Agencies and individuals on the
 subject.
6.         The Committee on Transport and Tourism visited Airports at Delhi, Mumbai, Goa, Chennai,
 Thiruvananthapuram, Guwahati and Ahmedabad to examine the functioning of these Airports and the facilities
 provided to the tourists at the airports.
The Committee was informed by the Airports Authority of India that they provide only tourism related facilities to the
 tourists at the airports which consists of paid/free facilities.
The Committee was also informed by the AAI that it manages five International airports namely Mumbai, Delhi,

 total of 120 airports in the country.

        Tourism is not only a major social  phenomenon of the modern society with enormous economic
 consequences but also  the world’s largest export industry, which accounts for about 8% of the total
 world’s exports, more than 30% of international trade in services, 10.7% of the  global work force and
 about 12% of world GDP.   It is also dubbed as the ‘Largest Smokeless Industry’ and contributes
 towards preservation of clean environment.
 2.Tourism is presently India’s second  largest net foreign exchange earning export industry after
 textiles/garments.  The estimated foreign exchange earning during January to December 99 were
 $2916.01 millions as compared to $2819.62 millions during the same period of  1998 showing an
 increase of 3.4%. Foreign tourist arrival has gone upto 2471848  during 1999 registering a growth of
 4.8% as compared to 1998.
 3.Tourism is of a particular significance  so far as India is concerned since it contributes to the
 environment and to the  national integration as it helps in the interaction amongst social and cultural
 lives of the people.   Over 160 million domestic  tourists visiting different parts of the country every
 year return with a  better understanding of the people living in the other regions of the country  and the
 cultural diversity of India.
 4.Tourism not only has the capacity to  generate large-scale employment opportunities in remote and
 backward areas but  also provides employment to a large number of women, both educated and
 uneducated.   In fact women are employed  in a large number in hotels, airlines services, travel agencies,
 handicrafts making, cultural and other tourism-related activities.
 5.The Ministry of Tourism functions as the  nodal agency for development of tourism in the country by
 coordinating and  supplementing the efforts of the State/Union Territory Governments, catalysing
 private investment, strengthening promotional and market efforts and in  providing trained manpower
 resources.
 6.The Ministry of Tourism has under its administrative control the following public sector
 undertaking/autonomous bodies:-
a)  India Tourism Development Corporation Limited;
b) National Council for Hotel Management and Catering  Technology;
 c) Indian Institute of Tourism & Travel Management;
d) Institutes of Hotel Management, Catering Technology and  Applied Nutrition at different locations in
 the country;
e)  Food Craft Institutes at different locations;
f)   Indian Institute of Skiing & Mountaineering;
g) National Institute of Water Sports.
 7.In  addition to the Head-quarters Organisation at New Delhi, the Directorate  General of Tourism has
 21 tourism offices in India and 18 tourist offices overseas.
 8. Demand No.82, containing the details of  budget allocations of Ministry of Tourism for the financial
 year 2000-2001, was considered by the Department-Related Parliamentary Standing Committee on
 Transport & Tourism at its meeting held on the 23rd March 2000.

            The Department-Related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Transport & Tourism at its meeting held on the
 27th June, 2000; inter-alia took note of the decision of the Cabinet Committee on Disinvestment with regard to
 disinvestment of Air India and decided to discuss the matter with the representatives of Ministry of Civil Aviation and
 Air India.  In connection with the subject, the Ministry of Civil Aviation have furnished a background note informing
 therein that the Disinvestment Commission, in its VIII Report submitted in August 1998, had recommended
 restructuring/disinvestment in Air India.  The main recommendations of the Commission are as under :-
(i)   Infusion of Government equity of Rs.1000 crores and finally bringing down the Government share holding in Air India
 to 40 per cent.
(ii)   Induction of a strategic partner holding 40 per cent equity on the basis of global bids.
(iii) 10 per cent equity to be offered to the domestic institutional investors and 10 per cent to retail investors and employees.
2.  The recommendations were considered extensively and in a meeting held on June 26, 1999 chaired by the former
 Finance Secretary and attended by the Secretary (Expenditure), Secretary (DPE) and Secretary (CA), the following
 decisions were taken:-
(i) The Government would presently be unable to infuse this amount into the airlines.
(ii) However, since the Government is unable to put in additional funds in the airlines, the process of disinvestment should
 not be stopped.
(iii) It was felt that a separate proposal should be submitted by Air India to the Department of Expenditure for infusion of
 Rs.110 crores interest subsidy for working capital for 1999-2000.
(iv)  It was decided that the Ministry of Civil Aviation would immediately take a note to the Cabinet Committee on
 Disinvestment in regard to disinvestment in Air India.
3. Subsequently, in December 1999, Government had set-up a separate Department namely the Department of
 Disinvestment under the Ministry of Finance.   The work regarding disinvestment has been transferred to that
 Department for further necessary action.
4.         The Cabinet Committee on Disinvestment (CCD) met on May 26, 2000 and considered the Note dated February
 12, 2000 submitted by the Department of Disinvestment and approved, in principle bringing down the equity of the
 Government of India in Air India to 40 per cent through a process of disinvestment by sale of 40 per cent of equity to a
 strategic partner, upto 10 per cent to employees and the balance by sale to financial institutions and/or on the share
 market.  The Committee further decided that in the event of the strategic partner being a joint venture with an element
 of foreign holding, the arrangement should be such as would limit foreign holding in Air India to a maximum of 26 per
 cent of the total equity.
4.1        The Cabinet Committee on Disinvestment (CCD) also approved that an Advisor be appointed to prepare a
 detailed scheme for disinvestment of Air India.
5.         An Inter Ministerial Group (IMG) has been constituted on May 30, 2000 with the following:-
1.      Shri Pradip Baijal, Secretary (Disinvestment).
2.      Shri Sanat Kaul, Joint Secretary, Ministry of Civil Aviation
3.      Shri S. Talwar, Joint Secretary, Deptt. Of Public Enterprises.
4.      Shri S.Behura, Joint Secretary, Deptt. Of Economic Affairs.
5.      Shri M.P. Mascarenhas, MD, Air India
6.      Shri S.Ranganathan, Director Finance, Air India.
6.         The first meeting of the Inter Ministerial Group was held on May 31, 2000.  In this meeting, a draft format of the
 advertisement for inviting Expressions of Interest from parties was approved.  It was also decided that presentation may

            Inland Waterways is an important mode of transport having potential for future development at places where
 Inland Traffic originate and terminates from the water front. At a time when the pollution caused by the vehicular
 traffic is playing havoc with the environment in India, the eco friendly inland waterways mode of transport can be of
 some help.  Unfortunately this important mode of transport have played little and negligible role in transportation of
 goods in India. The Central Inland Water Transport Corporation Ltd. is the only public sector undertaking, which has
 been engaged in the activity of transportation of cargo through inland Waterways in the country.  Besides it, the
 CIWTC has also been engaged in construction and repair of vessels. 
2.         The Department-Related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Transport & Tourism, in order to have a view of
 the problems of cargo transportation by Inland Waterways, decided to examine the functioning of the CIWTC.           
 The Committee heard the Secretary, Department of Shipping, Ministry of Surface Transport and the representatives of
 Central Inland Water Transport Corporation Ltd. (CIWTC), at its meeting held on 6
th July 2000, on the “Functioning
 and Revival of Central Inland Water Transport Corporation Ltd.” 
3.         The Committee was apprised that the Central Inland Water Transport Corporation Ltd., was set up as a
 Government of India Undertaking on 22
nd February, 1967 after taking over the assets and certain liabilities of the
 erstwhile River Steam Navigation Company Ltd. Under the orders of Calcutta High Court on 3rd May, 1967, the
 Corporation started functioning as an independent Company under the administrative control of the Ministry of Surface
 Transport from May 1967 and commenced its business from 5
th June 1967. The Corporation, which has 2626
 employees (as on 01.04.2000) on its pay roll, is headed by a full-time Chairman-cum-Managing Director, who is
 assisted by the Board of Directors. The principal activities of the Corporation includes:
Transportation by Inland Waterways from Calcutta to Bangladesh and to Assam (NW-II) and lighterage operations on
 the river Hooghly. 
Transportation by Inland Waterways from Calcutta to Allahabad    (NW-I) 
Construction and repair of small and medium sized vessels.
 Repair of ocean – going vessels. 
Ferry and Charter, General Engineering etc.
 4.         The Corporation has its Head Office at Calcutta.  There are three main divisions viz Rivers Service Division
 (RSD), Rajabagan Dock Yard (RBD) and Deep Sea Ship Repairs Division (DSSR).
RIVER SERVICES DIVISION (RSD) 
5.         It is the main earning division of the Corporation and engaged in riverine operations in Eastern (NW-I) and in
 the North Eastern (NW-II) regions of the country through Bangladesh.  The total number of employees in this division
 is 1300. 
6.            CIWTC is presently the principal IWT operator in the country with a fleet of 19 tugs (each capable of towing 2
 nos. 750 Tonnes capacity Dumb Barges), 16 nos. (600 Tonnes capacity each) self-propelled general cargo carriers, 3
 nos. self-propelled POL Tankers having average carrying capacity of 1350 Tonnes, 58 nos. (750 Tonnes capacity each)
 Dumb Barges and 5 nos.   Over Dimensional Cargo (ODC) carriers with average capacity of 500 Tonnes. 
The fleet of the company has been deployed for operation in the following routes:
 
Calcutta – Pandu – Guwahati – Calcutta on National Waterway-II serving Dhubri – Jogigopa – Pandu river stations. 
Calcutta – Karimganj – Calcutta serving Karimganj – Badarpur river stations. 
Calcutta – Bangladesh – Calcutta serving Khulna, Mongla and Narayanganj river stations in Bangladesh. 
Haldia – Calcutta – Patna – Varanasi – Allahabad on National Waterway No.1 route serving Farakka – Bhagalpur –
 Munger – Barauni Patna and Allahabad river stations.
 Sauger, Haldia, Diamond Harbour, Calcutta for lighterage operations.

CHARTERING AND MANAGEMENT OF FLIGHTS FOR HAJ PILGRIMS
            India is a multilingual, multicultural and multi-religious country.  A large number of people visit religious places
 within and outside the country.  Haj pilgrimage is also one such important annual event and every year a large number
 of people from India and all over the world visit Jeddah for Haj pilgrimage.  As per Government estimates, nearly
 72,000 people from India performed Haj pilgrimage in 2000 through the arrangement of the Central Haj Committee. 
2.         Before 1995, the transportation of Haj pilgrims to Jeddah and back was undertaken by air and sea.  The sea
 transportation was through Mugal Line Limited till June 1986, after which the Shipping Corporation of India Limited
 took over.  Some difficulties were faced in the provisioning of ships for Haj operations since this caused the diversion
 of the regular ships from the mainland-island services.  As the subsidy by sea passage was more than the subsidy for air
 passage, it was considered to continue Haj operations by air alone and stop sea travel altogether and since 1995 Haj
 pilgrims are being transported to Jeddah by air only. 
3.         The Ministry of Civil Aviation, while giving the details of history of Haj operations, informed the Committee
 that as a policy, the Government of India has been subsidizing the Haj charter operations to facilitate performance of
 Haj pilgrimage even by socio-economically weaker sections of Society.  The amount charged as airfare from the
 pilgrims has more or less remained the same in the last ten years whereas the Government’s subsidy has shown a
 tremendous increase.  The information regarding the number of pilgrims, number of flights, fares and the subsidy per
 pilgrim since 1991 is as under:-

            Lighthouse is a real guide of the mariners in vast ocean.  Lighthouses play an important role in guiding the
 mariners and fixing their position in the sea.  The term “Lighthouse” represents all aids to navigation, including light
 vessels, sound signals, buoys, beacons for any mark, sign or apparatus, radio aids such as Differential Global
 Positioning System Racons, Loran – C, Radio Beacons etc.  The Department of Lighthouses and Lightships is premier
 agency in India and provides all aids to marine navigation during harbour phase for mariners in Indian waters. 
2.         The Lighthouses are defined as ‘General’ and ‘Local’.  The lighthouses under the Central Government and
 notified in the Official Gazette are the ‘General Lighthouses’ which come under the authority of the Department of
 Lighthouses and Lightships.  The responsibility of establishment, operation and maintenance of the lighthouses lies
 with the Department.  The ‘Local’ Lighthouses are those which are under the State Governments or the Port Trusts for
 guiding the ships while entering/leaving the Ports.  However as per the Lighthouse Act, the Department is empowered
 to inspect a local lighthouse and advise the concerned authority for its improvement. 
3.         The Department of Lighthouses and Lightships consisting of 167 Lighthouses, 12 Deep Sea Buoys, 10
 Differential Global Positioning Systems, 4 Decca Navigator Chain Stations, 6 LORAN –C Stations and 29 Racons
 covering the coastal length of over 7000 kms.  The Department would be adding 5 major Lighthouses-2 along the
 Andhra Coast and 3 in the Palk Bay.    Apart from the new Lighthouses and Radio Aids to navigation, the Department
 has up graded the old and pre-independent equipments with the latest state-of-art equipments.  
4.         The Department of Lighthouses and Lightships is a subordinate office under the Ministry of Shipping and
 headed by the Director General of Lighthouses and Lightships.  The Headquarters of the Department of Lighthouses
 and Lightships is situated at Noida. 
5.         The Indian coast has been divided into six regions known as Lighthouse Districts.  The area covered and
 facilities available at Regional Headquarters are as under: - 
(i)            Jamnagar -      is the regional headquarters of Saurashtra & Kachchh Lighthouse District stretching from
 Jakhau Lighthouse near Pakistan border to Bhavnagar.  The region caters to the ‘Aids to Navigation’ requirements of
 two peninsulas, namely the Gulf of Kachchh and the Gulf of Khamabat.  The vessels approaching Kandla Port and a
 number of minor ports under the aegis of Gujarat Maritime Board take the help of various Aids established in this
 region. 
(ii)            Mumbai - is the regional headquarter for Mumbai Lighthouses District stretching from Hazira Lighthouses to
 Suratkal Lighthouses near Mangalore.  The region meets the navigational requirements of Major Ports at Mumbai,
 JNPT, Mormugao and new Mangalore.  In addition the various aids established by this region also caters to the needs of
 minor ports of Gujarat Maritime Board established on the eastern bank of the Gulf of Khambat and Maharashtra
 Maritime Board. 
(iii)       Cochin - is the regional headquarter for the Cochin Lighthouse District stretching from Kasaragod to
 Manakodam and all the Lighthouses in the Lakshadweep Island.  The region meets the navigational requirements of the
 Major Port of Kochi and number of minor ports of Karnataka and Kerala. 
(iv)            Chennai - is the regional headquarters for the Chennai Lighthouse District stretching from Alleppey on the
 west coast to Kanyakumari and Kanyakumari to Machhlipatnam on the east coast.  The region meets the navigational
 requirement of a number of ports under Maritimes Boards of  Tamilnadu and  Andhra Pradesh and the ship breaking
 yard to Vodarevu. 
(v)            Kolkata - is the regional headquarters of the Kolkata Lighthouses District stretching from Antervedi
 (Narsapur) to Saugar Island.  The District caters to the need of the shipping traffic for Vishakhapatnam Port, Hoogly
 Dock and Port and a number of ports under Andhra Pradesh Martime Board and West Bengal Maritime Board. 
(vi)            Andaman & Nicobar Islands:- Port Blair is the regional headquarters of Andaman & Nicobar groups of

            Tourism has emerged as one of the world’s most important activities.  It is the world’s largest export industry. 
 According to the World Tourism Organisation, about 663 million tourists travelled internationally in 1999 and spent
 about US$ 453 billion.  The figures indicate that tourism has certainly become a major social phenomenon of the
 modern society with enormous economic consequences.  Its importance as an instrument for economic development
 and employment generation, particularly in remote and backward areas, has been now well recognized the world over. 
2.         Travel and tourism related jobs/employment are not only generated at a relatively low cost and concentrated in
 small business and local community but also provide significant opportunities for women and young people, offer
 educational training and skill development and protect and revitalize traditional arts and crafts. 
3.         India is a country of continental dimensions with a fascinating kaleidoscope of diverse races, languages,
 religions, customs and traditions.  The tourist attractions of India include historical monuments, places of religious
 importance, mountain and beach resorts, wildlife and interesting eco-systems etc.  Tourism is presently India’s third
 largest export industry-after readymade garments and gem and jewellery.  The international tourist traffic to the country
 during 1951 was just 16,829. Over a period of about 50 years, the arrivals increased to 264 million in 2000 and
 registered a compounded annual rate of growth of about 11 percent.  The foreign tourist arrivals to India and the
 estimated foreign exchange earnings through tourism along with growth rate for the year 1997 to 2000 are as under: -
Growth Rate (%)
It is, therefore, evident that the rate of growth in foreign exchange earning from tourism is exceptionally high and is
 expected to become even higher in the coming years.
 
4.         The Ministry of Tourism has been declared as Ministry of Tourism and Culture, Department of Tourism w.e.f.
 27
th May 2000.  The Department of Tourism is the nodal agency for the formulation of national policies and
 programmes and for the coordination of activities of various Central Government Agencies, State Governments/UTs
 and the Private Sector for the development and promotion of tourism in the country.  The role of the Department of
 Tourism has been to coordinate and supplement the efforts of the State/U.T. Governments in development of tourism
 through Central financial assistance, to catalyze private investment, strengthen promotional and marketing efforts and
 to provide trained manpower resources.  The administrative head of the Department is the Secretary (Tourism).  The
 Department is assisted by an attached office headed by the Director General.  The office of the Director General of
 Tourism provides executive directions for the implementation of various policies and programmes.  Directorate General
 of Tourism has a field formation of 21 offices within the country and 18 offices abroad.  The overseas offices are
 primarily responsible for tourism promotion and marketing in their respective areas and the field offices in India are
 responsible for providing information service to tourists and to monitor the progress of field projects. 
5.         The Department of Tourism has the following public sector undertaking/autonomous institutions under its
 administrative control:-

National Institute of Water Sports (NIWS).

 coordination with all the relevant agencies so as to achieve synergy in the development of tourism.  The development
 activities during the Plan would give necessary emphasis to environment protection and cultural preservation.  The
 thrust areas during Ninth Plan period are:- 
Infrastructure development

file:///C/Users/user/Desktop/pri/Committee%20on%20Transport,%20Tourism%20and%20Culture/49threport.htm[28-08-2018 12:52:10]
REPORT 
 
            The Department of Culture primarily deals with the tangible and intangible heritage.  In a larger perspective, it
 also addresses the issues relating to the history, values and beliefs in conjunction with several other Ministries and
 Departments.  Culture being considered one of the keys to Human Resource Development, in the Five Year Plans,
 suitable emphasis was laid on development of Culture from the grass roots.  Relentless efforts made in various fields of
 Culture have started bearing fruit.  A number of institutions have been actively associated with the promotion,
 preservation and dissemination of the rich cultural heritage of India. 
2.         The Department of Culture was set up in 1985 through the 174
th Amendment of the Government of India
 (Allocation of Business) Rules, 1961.  It was part of the Ministry of Human Resource Development before its transfer
 to the Ministry of Culture, Youth Affairs and Sport.  Since 27th May 2000, it forms part of the Ministry of Tourism and
 Culture and is known as the Department of Culture.  The Department is responsible to promote art and cultural mutual
 understanding and goodwill and foster closer relations with foreign countries.  Preservation of ancient and historic
 monuments and records, exploration and excavation of archaeological sites and remains, maintenance and expansion of
 libraries and museums of national importance and observance of centenaries and anniversaries of eminent personalities
 are among its other responsibilities. 
3.         The main functions/activities of the Department can be broadly classified under the following heads:- 
Maintenance and Conservation of heritage, ancient monuments and historic sites.
Administration of Museums and Libraries.
Observing Centenaries and anniversaries of important national personalities and events.
Promoting institutions and organisations of Buddhist and Tibetan Studies.
Entering into cultural agreements with foreign countries and holding of Festival of India abroad.
Anthropology and Ethnology.
Archives and Archival Libraries.
Academies and National School of Drama.
Promotion and dissemination of Culture.
Memorials.
 
4.         The Committee was also informed that while full attention will be given to all the above mentioned sectors,
 activities of the department will be particularly focused on:- 
Conservation and preservation of cultural heritage;
Schemes of the National Cultural fund;
Linkage between education and culture;
Development of a public library movement;
Strengthening of Museums and Art Galleries; and
Promotion of Culture and dissemination. 
5.         The Committee appreciates the decision of the Government to bring Department of Tourism and Culture within
 the purview of one Ministry.    The Committee feels that Culture and Tourism are interdependent and interrelated
 subjects.  India is having enormous monuments, museums, historical spots, and palaces etc., which need to be exploited
 from the tourism point of view.  The Government should have considered to keep both the Departments together very
 long back, so that synergy between the two Departments would have been achieved. Sooner or later now Government
 have realized and brought the two Departments under one Ministry. Most of the cultural sites, monuments, etc. are
 attractive spots of the tourist interest.  The Committee also feels that the coordination between Department of Culture
 and Tourism is very important for proper utilisation of the tourist value of the Cultural spots/monuments. A number of
 times, the Committee has observed that there has been contradiction in the approach of the two departments.  The
 Department of Tourism is interested in having more and more tourists whereas the Department of Culture, particularly
 ASI, discourages the tourists with a view to preserve/protect the monuments.  The Committee recommends that the two
 departments should try to achieve equilibrium between the approaches of preservation/ protection of monuments and
 arrival of tourists to these monuments.  Since the Departments of Tourism and Culture are now the parts of the same
 Ministry, the Committee hopes that a higher level of synergy will be achieved by doing away their differences.

 Tourism and for the coordination of activities of various Central Government agencies, State Governments/UTs and the
 Private Sector for the development and promotion of tourism in the country.  The Department of Tourism plays a
 crucial role in coordinating and supplementing the efforts of the State/Union Territory Governments catalyzing
 investment, strengthening promotional and marketing efforts and private in providing training manpower resources.
 The main activities of the Department are: -
 
i)
                  Policy formulation and planning
ii)                Co-ordination
iii)               Regulation
iv)              Infrastructure and Product development
v)                Human Resource Development
vi)              Publicity, Marketing and Facilitation

 INTRODUCTION
 
         I, the Chairman, Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Transport, Tourism and Culture,
 having been authorised by the Committee to present on its behalf, do hereby present this Eighty-third report on
 “Functioning of the Commission of Railway Safety”.
 
2.      The Committee considered the subject and held discussions with the representatives of Ministry of Civil Aviation
 and Commission of Railway Safety at Bangalore and Lucknow during its study visits in September 2001 and
 September 2002 respectively.  The Committee took oral evidence of the officers of Ministry of Civil Aviation and
 Commission of Railway Safety at its meeting held on    20
th May 2003.  The Committee also took oral evidence of the
 representatives of Ministry of Railways at its meeting held on the 14th July 2003.
 
3.         3.         In order to get wider views on the subject, the Committee invited the views of individuals and institutions
 interested in the subject through advertisement in all major national dailies and vernacular newspapers all over the
 country.  The advertisement evoked tremendous public response and the Committee received memoranda on various
 aspects of the functioning of the Commission of Railway Safety from a lot of people including many retired
 Commissioners/Chief Commissioners of Railway Safety.  The Committee also heard the views of Shri Prakash Narain
 and Shri R.N. Malhotra, both former Chairmen, Railway Board and Shri Arya Bhushan, former Chief Commissioner of
 Railway Safety in connection with the subject.
 
4.      The Committee wishes to express its thanks to the officers of Ministry of Civil Aviation, Commission of Railway
 Safety and Ministry of Railways for placing before the Committee the material and information desired in connection
 with the subject and for clarifying the points raised by the Members.  The Committee also acknowledges the
 contribution of Shri Prakash Narain, Shri R.N. Malhotra and Shri Arya Bhushan, who submitted their valuable

I, the Chairperson, Standing Committee on Water Resources (2019 -20) having been 
authorized by the Committee to submit the Report on their behalf, present the First Report on 
Demands for Grants (2019 -20) of the Ministry of Jal Shakti - Department of Water R esources, 
River Development and Ganga Rejuvenation. 
 
2. The Demands for Grants have been examined by the Committee under  Rule  
331E(1)(a) of the Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business in Lok  Sabha. 
 
3. The Committee took evidence of the representatives of the Ministry of Jal Shakti - 
Department of Water Resources, River Development and Ganga Rejuvenation on  23.10.2019.

29.11.2019.

Shakti - Department of Water Resources, River Development and Ganga Rejuvenation for 
providing them the requisite written material and for making oral depositi ons before the 
Committee in connection with the examination of the subject. 
 
6. The Committee would also like to place on record their sense of deep appreciation for 
the assistance rendered to them by the officials of the Lok Sabha Secretariat attached to the  
Committee.
